disease.name: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)
disease.scientific_name: Irritable Bowel Syndrome / Functional Bowel Disorder / Spastic Colon
disease.icd_10_code: K58 (Irritable bowel syndrome); K58.0 (IBS with diarrhoea); K58.1 (IBS with constipation); K58.2 (IBS with mixed bowel habits); K58.8 (Other IBS); K58.9 (IBS without diarrhoea — unspecified)
disease.category: Functional Gastrointestinal Disorder / Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction (DGBI)

overview.description: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a common, chronic, relapsing functional gastrointestinal (GI) disorder characterised by recurrent abdominal pain or discomfort associated with alterations in bowel habits — diarrhoea, constipation, or an alternating pattern of both — in the absence of identifiable structural, biochemical, or organic disease to explain the symptoms. IBS is classified as a Disorder of Gut-Brain Interaction (DGBI), reflecting current understanding that symptoms arise from dysregulation of the bidirectional communication between the enteric nervous system (the 'gut brain'), the central nervous system, and gut microbiome — rather than from structural damage to the bowel. It is the most commonly diagnosed gastrointestinal condition globally and one of the leading reasons for gastroenterology outpatient referrals.
overview.affected_organ: Large intestine (colon) primarily; also small intestine and the gut-brain axis (enteric and central nervous systems)
overview.prevalence: Affects approximately 10-15% of adults globally; up to 20% in some populations. Approximately 40-50 million people in the USA; estimated 15-20 million in India (possibly higher due to underdiagnosis). Most common GI diagnosis in primary care.
overview.age_group: Most common in adults aged 18-50 years; peak presentation in 20s-30s; can occur at any age including children and elderly. Symptoms often begin in adolescence.
overview.sex_ratio: Women affected 2-3 times more frequently than men in high-income countries. In South Asian countries, male predominance has been reported in some studies — possibly reflecting healthcare-seeking behaviour differences.
overview.key_fact: IBS does NOT cause structural damage to the intestine, does NOT increase risk of bowel cancer, and does NOT progress to inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's or ulcerative colitis) — but it significantly impairs quality of life and is underdiagnosed and underrecognised globally.

gut_brain_axis.description: The gut-brain axis is a bidirectional communication network between the enteric nervous system (ENS — over 500 million neurons in the gut wall; sometimes called the 'second brain'), the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), the autonomic nervous system, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and the gut microbiome. In IBS, this axis is dysregulated — resulting in: altered gut motility, visceral hypersensitivity (exaggerated pain responses to normal bowel stimuli), abnormal gut secretion, and immune activation.
gut_brain_axis.serotonin_role: Over 90-95% of the body's serotonin (5-HT) is produced in the gut by enterochromaffin cells. Serotonin regulates gut motility, secretion, and pain signalling. IBS-D: excess serotonin causes rapid transit; IBS-C: serotonin deficiency causes slow transit. 5-HT3 antagonists (IBS-D) and 5-HT4 agonists (IBS-C) target this pathway.
gut_brain_axis.microbiome_connection: The gut microbiome communicates with the brain via: vagal nerve signalling, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, enteroendocrine cell signalling, immune modulation, and serotonin production. IBS patients show distinct microbiome profiles — reduced diversity, altered Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio, and reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations.

types.name: IBS with Predominant Constipation (IBS-C)
types.description: Characterised by hard, lumpy stools and infrequent bowel movements. Patients have Bristol Stool Form Scale (BSFS) type 1-2 (hard pellets or lumpy sausage) in ≥25% of bowel movements AND type 6-7 (mushy or watery) in <25%. Abdominal pain, bloating, and distension are prominent. Straining and sensation of incomplete evacuation are common.
types.bsfs: Type 1 (separate hard lumps like nuts) and Type 2 (sausage-shaped but lumpy) predominate
types.management: Soluble fibre, osmotic laxatives, linaclotide, lubiprostone, prucalopride, low FODMAP diet

types.name: IBS with Predominant Diarrhoea (IBS-D)
types.description: Characterised by loose, watery, frequent stools with urgency. BSFS type 6-7 (mushy or watery) in ≥25% AND type 1-2 in <25% of bowel movements. Often associated with severe urgency, post-prandial (after eating) bowel movements, and anxiety about being near a toilet. Faecal incontinence may occur in severe cases.
types.bsfs: Type 6 (fluffy pieces with ragged edges — mushy stool) and Type 7 (watery, no solid pieces) predominate
types.management: Low FODMAP diet, loperamide, antispasmodics, rifaximin, 5-HT3 antagonists (alosetron, ondansetron), low-dose TCAs, bile acid sequestrants (if BAM suspected)
types.note: Bile acid malabsorption (BAM) mimics IBS-D and is commonly misdiagnosed as IBS — SeHCAT test or 7alphaC4 serum test can diagnose; responds to bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colesevelam)

types.name: IBS with Mixed Bowel Habits (IBS-M)
types.description: Also called IBS-Mixed type — patients experience BOTH hard/lumpy stools (BSFS 1-2) AND loose/watery stools (BSFS 6-7) in ≥25% of bowel movements. The alternating pattern is unpredictable and particularly difficult for patients — alternating between constipation and diarrhoea within days or weeks.
types.management: Most challenging subtype to treat; tailor treatment to predominant current symptom; low FODMAP diet; antispasmodics; neuromodulators

types.name: IBS Unsubtyped (IBS-U)
types.description: Meets Rome IV criteria for IBS but stool consistency abnormalities are insufficient to fit IBS-C, IBS-D, or IBS-M subtypes. Patients with variable symptoms that do not clearly predominate into any category.
types.management: General IBS management; symptom-directed treatment; low FODMAP diet; antispasmodics

types.name: Post-Infectious IBS (PI-IBS)
types.description: IBS developing after a clearly documented episode of acute gastroenteritis (bacterial, viral, or parasitic). Approximately 10-15% of patients who suffer gastroenteritis develop PI-IBS. Onset is acute — symptoms begin within days to weeks after the infection and persist. The most common subtype is IBS-D after infection. Campylobacter jejuni, Salmonella, Shigella, norovirus, and Giardia are the most common precipitants. Mechanisms include mucosal immune activation, increased intestinal permeability, enteric nervous system damage, and altered microbiome.
types.risk_factors: Severity of initial infection, female sex, younger age, psychological comorbidity (anxiety, depression at time of infection), antibiotic exposure during infection
types.prognosis: PI-IBS often improves over 1-3 years without specific treatment; recovery rate ~50% at 6 years
types.management: Same as general IBS; probiotics may be particularly beneficial (microbiome restoration); rifaximin has evidence

types.name: IBS Overlapping with Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)
types.description: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth — excessive bacteria in the small intestine (normally near-sterile) — produces bloating, gas, diarrhoea, and abdominal pain identical to IBS. Estimated 30-84% of IBS patients have SIBO on hydrogen breath testing (though diagnostic accuracy debated). Causes: reduced gastric acid (PPIs), motility disorders, structural abnormalities, prior surgery. SIBO-IBS responds to gut-selective antibiotics (rifaximin).
types.diagnosis: Lactulose or glucose hydrogen breath test; small intestinal aspirate culture (gold standard but invasive)
types.management: Rifaximin 550mg TDS × 14 days (first-line for non-constipated IBS with bloating — also targets SIBO); repeat courses for recurrence; prokinetics to prevent recurrence

types.name: IBS with Bile Acid Malabsorption (BAM-IBS)
types.description: Bile acid malabsorption (BAM) — failure of terminal ileum to reabsorb bile acids — causes them to enter the colon where they stimulate water and electrolyte secretion, accelerate transit, and cause chronic watery diarrhoea. BAM is present in 25-33% of patients diagnosed with IBS-D and is frequently misdiagnosed as functional IBS-D. Should always be considered in IBS-D patients, especially post-cholecystectomy or with prior terminal ileum disease.
types.diagnosis: SeHCAT (75-selenium homocholic acid taurine) scan — most accurate test; serum 7alphaC4 (fasting); faecal bile acid measurement
types.management: Bile acid sequestrants: cholestyramine (4g 1-4 times daily), colesevelam (625mg 3-6 daily), colestipol; responds dramatically to treatment — diagnosis of BAM is therefore important

types.name: IBS with Psychological Comorbidities (Severe IBS)
types.description: A significant subset of IBS patients — particularly those with severe or refractory symptoms — have significant psychological comorbidity: depression, anxiety, somatic symptom disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), or history of physical or sexual abuse. These patients often have enhanced central pain sensitisation, more severe visceral hypersensitivity, more frequent healthcare utilisation, and poorer response to peripheral GI treatments alone. Central neuromodulators and psychological therapies are most effective in this group.
types.prevalence: Moderate to severe anxiety: ~60% of IBS patients in clinic; depression: ~40%; PTSD: 30-40% of referred IBS patients
types.management: Psychological therapies (CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy) most evidence-based; low-dose TCAs or SSRIs; multidisciplinary approach with gastroenterologist and psychologist

severity_levels.name: Mild IBS
severity_levels.description: Infrequent symptoms causing mild distress; minimal impact on quality of life
severity_levels.ibs_sss_score: <175 (IBS Symptom Severity Score — validated questionnaire assessing pain severity, frequency, bloating, bowel habit satisfaction, life interference)
severity_levels.quality_of_life: Minor impact; able to work and socialise normally; adapts food and lifestyle without significant restriction
severity_levels.psychological: No or minimal anxiety/depression about symptoms
severity_levels.management: Dietary advice (low FODMAP); lifestyle education; reassurance; antispasmodics (peppermint oil, mebeverine) PRN; first consultation may not need medication

severity_levels.name: Moderate IBS
severity_levels.description: Regular symptoms causing significant distress and impacting daily activities
severity_levels.frequency: Symptoms most days; predictable triggers but still significant interference
severity_levels.quality_of_life: Significant — affects work attendance, social plans, travel; avoidance behaviours developing
severity_levels.psychological: Moderate health anxiety; frustration; some social anxiety related to bowel symptoms
severity_levels.management: Low FODMAP diet (with dietitian); antispasmodics regularly; IBS-D: loperamide, rifaximin; IBS-C: linaclotide, lactulose; consider low-dose TCA; GP or gastroenterology review; NICE recommends 12 months of GP management before specialist referral

severity_levels.name: Severe IBS
severity_levels.description: Frequent, disabling symptoms with major impact on all aspects of life — work, relationships, social activities, mental health
severity_levels.frequency: Near-daily symptoms; severe pain episodes; significant bowel urgency or constipation
severity_levels.quality_of_life: Severely impaired — significant loss of work days (presenteeism and absenteeism); avoidance of social activities, travel, eating out; relationship strain
severity_levels.psychological: High levels of anxiety, depression, catastrophising; significant impact on mental health; possible PTSD/abuse history
severity_levels.management: Specialist gastroenterology referral; comprehensive Rome IV-based assessment; exclude organic disease fully; psychological therapy (CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy); neuromodulators (TCAs, SNRIs, SSRIs); multidisciplinary team approach; biofeedback; consider specialist IBS nurse

visceral_hypersensitivity.description: The hallmark mechanism of IBS — IBS patients have a lowered threshold for pain in response to gut stimuli that would not normally be painful. Rectal balloon distension studies show IBS patients report pain at lower volumes than healthy controls. This heightened sensitivity involves both peripheral sensitisation (enteric nervous system) and central sensitisation (altered pain processing in brain and spinal cord).
visceral_hypersensitivity.peripheral_component: Mast cell activation in gut mucosa releases histamine and tryptase → activates sensory nerves (TRPV1 channels, PAR2 receptors) → enhanced pain signalling to spinal cord
visceral_hypersensitivity.central_component: Descending pain inhibitory pathways are deficient; enhanced pain facilitation; increased activation of anterior cingulate cortex and limbic system on gut stimulation (neuroimaging)

altered_gut_motility.description: Gut transit time is significantly altered in IBS subtypes: IBS-D: accelerated small intestinal and colonic transit; IBS-C: significantly delayed colonic transit; IBS-M: variable. High-amplitude propagated contractions (HAPCs) are increased in IBS-D.
altered_gut_motility.serotonin_axis: Serotonin (5-HT) from enterochromaffin cells regulates gut motility — excess in IBS-D causes rapid transit; deficiency in IBS-C causes slow transit. Abnormal 5-HT reuptake transporter (SERT) expression found in IBS

gut_microbiome_dysbiosis.description: IBS patients demonstrate distinct gut microbiome profiles compared to healthy controls — reduced diversity, altered Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio, reduced Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, increased Proteobacteria, Ruminococcaceae, and Lachnospiraceae. This dysbiosis may precede IBS onset (PI-IBS context) or develop secondary to dietary changes.
mechanisms: Produces excess fermentation gases (hydrogen, methane, hydrogen sulphide) causing bloating and altered motility
Bacterial metabolites activate mucosal immune cells and sensory nerves
Altered SCFA production reduces colonocyte nutrition and mucosal integrity

intestinal_permeability.description: Increased intestinal permeability ('leaky gut') — disruption of tight junctions between intestinal epithelial cells — allows bacteria, bacterial products (LPS), and food antigens to cross the mucosal barrier → activates mucosal immune system → low-grade mucosal inflammation → sensory nerve activation → visceral hypersensitivity and altered motility. Identified in PI-IBS, stress-induced IBS, and in many IBS-D patients.
intestinal_permeability.triggers: Psychological stress; prior infection; alcohol; NSAIDs; dysbiosis; food intolerances

immune_activation.description: Low-grade mucosal immune activation is demonstrated in many IBS patients: increased mucosal mast cells (particularly adjacent to enteric nerves — promoting visceral hypersensitivity); increased CD4+ T cells; elevated mucosal cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α); increased IgE-mediated food sensitisation (especially in IBS-D). Distinct from the transmural inflammation of IBD (Crohn's/UC) — the immune activation in IBS is subtle and patchy.
immune_activation.note: Faecal calprotectin is typically NORMAL or mildly elevated in IBS (vs significantly elevated in IBD) — important diagnostic distinction

gut_brain_dysregulation.description: Bidirectional gut-brain axis dysfunction: stress → HPA axis activation → corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) → increased gut permeability, accelerated colonic transit, mast cell activation → gut symptoms. Conversely, gut symptoms send pain signals to the brain → anxiety, hypervigilance, catastrophising → amplified pain perception → increased gut symptoms (vicious cycle).
gut_brain_dysregulation.stress_effects: Acute stress: accelerates gut transit (IBS-D like); chronic stress: alters microbiome, increases permeability, promotes inflammation. Cortisol directly activates colonic CRF receptors causing motility changes.

triggers: FODMAPs — Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides And Polyols: poorly absorbed short-chain carbohydrates fermented by colonic bacteria producing gas, bloating, and osmotic diarrhoea. The most clinically validated dietary trigger in IBS.
Wheat and gluten (fructans in wheat, not gluten itself, are the primary FODMAP trigger in most IBS patients; true coeliac disease must be excluded)
Lactose (milk sugar) — malabsorption causes bloating, gas, and diarrhoea; more common in South Asian populations
Fructose malabsorption (excess fructose in apples, pears, mangoes, high-fructose corn syrup)
Fatty meals — stimulate gut motility via CCK release; worsen post-prandial symptoms
Caffeine — accelerates colonic transit; stimulates gut motility
Alcohol — disrupts gut barrier; accelerates transit
Spicy foods — capsaicin activates TRPV1 receptors on gut nociceptors
Large meal volumes — gastrocolic reflex magnified in IBS (exaggerated response to gastric distension)
Psychological stress (work pressure, relationship problems, bereavement, examinations) — most consistently reported trigger
Anxiety and worry — activates HPA axis and sympathetic nervous system → gut motility changes
Sleep deprivation — worsens gut pain sensitivity and increases inflammatory markers
Travel — change in routine, food, and water disrupts gut microbiome and function
Menstruation — cyclical hormone changes worsen IBS symptoms; progesterone slows transit (IBS-C worsening); prostaglandins worsen IBS-D
Prior gastroenteritis — PI-IBS (10-15% develop IBS after GI infection)
Antibiotic use — disrupts gut microbiome; promotes dysbiosis and SIBO
Physical illness or surgery — post-surgical gut function changes
Hormonal fluctuations — menstrual cycle; pregnancy; menopause
Intercurrent illness — upper respiratory infections worsen IBS
Proton pump inhibitor use — reduces gastric acid allowing bacterial overgrowth

risk_factors: Female sex (2-3x higher prevalence in women)
Young to middle age (18-50 years peak)
Family history of IBS (genetic component — 2-3x increased risk in first-degree relatives)
Psychological disorders: anxiety, depression, panic disorder, PTSD (bidirectional relationship)
History of physical, sexual, or emotional abuse (childhood or adult)
Prior GI infection (PI-IBS risk — Campylobacter, Salmonella, norovirus, Giardia)
Atopy, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome (conditions that frequently overlap with IBS)
genetic_factors: Heritability estimated at 40-50% from twin studies; concordance higher in monozygotic than dizygotic twins
SERT (serotonin transporter) gene variants (SLC6A4 promoter polymorphism) — affect serotonin reuptake and transit
SCN5A gene mutations (voltage-gated sodium channel) — found in a subset of IBS-C patients; affects gut smooth muscle
Immune gene variants: IL-10 promoter, TNF-alpha, TNFSF15 — affect mucosal immune regulation
GI sensory genes: TRPV1 variants affecting visceral pain threshold

rome_iv_diagnostic_criteria.main_criterion: Recurrent abdominal pain, on average at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, associated with two or more of the following criteria:
criteria_list: Related to defecation — pain improves (or occasionally worsens) with bowel movement
Associated with a change in frequency of stool — more or less frequent stools when pain occurs
Associated with a change in form (appearance) of stool — harder, softer, or different consistency during pain episodes
rome_iv_diagnostic_criteria.onset: Symptom onset at least 6 months prior to diagnosis
rome_iv_diagnostic_criteria.diagnosis_type: POSITIVE clinical diagnosis — NOT a diagnosis of exclusion (Rome IV 2016 guidance). IBS should be diagnosed on clinical grounds once alarm features are excluded, without extensive investigation in all patients.

bristol_stool_form_scale.description: The Bristol Stool Form Scale (BSFS) is the universally used validated clinical tool for categorising stool consistency — important for IBS subtyping.
types: Type 1: Separate hard lumps like nuts — very constipated
Type 3: Sausage-shaped with cracks on surface — normal
Type 4: Sausage or snake, smooth and soft — ideal normal
Type 5: Soft blobs with clear-cut edges — tending towards diarrhoea
Type 6: Fluffy pieces with ragged edges, mushy — diarrhoea
Type 7: Watery, no solid pieces, entirely liquid — severe diarrhoea

primary_symptoms.name: Recurrent Abdominal Pain and Cramping
primary_symptoms.description: The defining symptom of IBS — a mandatory requirement for Rome IV diagnosis. Characteristically described as: cramping, colicky, or aching abdominal pain. Most commonly localised to the lower abdomen (hypogastrium and left or right iliac fossae) but may occur anywhere. Classically relieved (or less commonly worsened) by defecation. Onset often post-prandial (30-60 minutes after eating — from the gastrocolic reflex). Severity ranges from dull discomfort to severe, incapacitating cramps. Typically does NOT wake patients from sleep (nocturnal symptoms are an alarm feature).
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Severe (varies between patients and episodes)
primary_symptoms.onset: Post-prandial (30-60 min after meals) or associated with bowel urgency; not typically nocturnal
primary_symptoms.characteristically_better_with: Passage of stool or flatus; heat (hot water bottle); antispasmodics
primary_symptoms.characteristically_worse_with: Eating (especially high FODMAP foods or fatty meals); stress and anxiety; menstruation (in women)

primary_symptoms.name: Bloating and Abdominal Distension
primary_symptoms.description: The most distressing symptom for many IBS patients — often reported as MORE bothersome than pain. Bloating is the subjective sensation of increased abdominal pressure, tightness, or fullness. Distension refers to the objective, measurable increase in abdominal girth (up to 10-12cm increase during the day). Results from: excess gas production from FODMAP fermentation; visceral hypersensitivity to normal gas volumes; altered gas handling (IBS patients cannot propel gas caudally as efficiently); abnormal abdomino-phrenic accommodation reflex (diaphragm descends and anterior abdominal wall protrudes).
primary_symptoms.pattern: Typically worsens throughout the day; minimal in the morning; maximal by evening; improves overnight
primary_symptoms.note: Gas volume in IBS is NOT significantly higher than normal controls — it is the inability to handle normal gas and the heightened sensitivity to it that causes symptoms

primary_symptoms.name: Altered Bowel Habits — Diarrhoea (IBS-D)
primary_symptoms.description: Loose, watery, frequent bowel movements — often BSFS type 6-7. Characteristic features: urgency (sudden compelling need to defecate — may be socially incapacitating); post-prandial urgency (need to defecate immediately after eating); multiple loose stools in the morning ('morning rush'); faecal urgency and occasionally urgency incontinence; stools typically do NOT contain blood (blood = alarm feature). Nocturnal diarrhoea is unusual in IBS and warrants investigation for IBD.
primary_symptoms.pattern: Classically worst in morning; post-prandially; triggered by stress

primary_symptoms.name: Altered Bowel Habits — Constipation (IBS-C)
primary_symptoms.description: Hard, infrequent stools — BSFS type 1-2. Features: straining; sensation of incomplete evacuation; passage of small, hard rabbit pellets; defecation ≤3 times per week; need to use manual manoeuvres (digitation — manual evacuation). In IBS-C, the pain is the key differentiating feature from functional constipation (which has no significant abdominal pain).
primary_symptoms.distinction: IBS-C: BOTH constipation AND significant abdominal pain — this combination distinguishes it from simple functional constipation (which lacks pain)

primary_symptoms.name: Mucus in Stool
primary_symptoms.description: Passage of white or clear mucus (not blood) per rectum — very common in IBS, particularly IBS-D and IBS-M. Results from hypersecretion of intestinal mucus from goblet cells in response to mucosal irritation. A reassuring and characteristic IBS feature — mucus alone (without blood) is benign.
primary_symptoms.note: WHITE or CLEAR mucus = benign (IBS); BLOODY mucus = alarm feature requiring urgent investigation (IBD, colorectal cancer, infective colitis)

primary_symptoms.name: Sensation of Incomplete Evacuation (Tenesmus)
primary_symptoms.description: Feeling that the bowel has not emptied completely after defecation — a very common and distressing IBS symptom. Causes repeated return to the toilet. Results from: visceral hypersensitivity creating a false sense of rectal fullness; pelvic floor dysfunction (dyssynergia); true incomplete rectal emptying from hard stools (IBS-C). Particularly prominent in IBS-D and IBS-M.

secondary_symptoms: Excessive flatulence and wind — from FODMAP fermentation; socially embarrassing; exacerbates bloating
Faecal urgency — sudden need to defecate that may be difficult to defer (especially IBS-D); fear of incontinence profoundly affects quality of life
Nausea — particularly post-prandial; associated with IBS-D; may be related to gut dysmotility
Fatigue and lethargy — disproportionate to apparent bowel symptoms; one of the most impactful symptoms for quality of life; possibly related to disrupted sleep and central sensitisation
Headache — more frequent in IBS than general population; possible central sensitisation overlap
Back pain — particularly lower back; visceral-somatic pain referral from bowel to back
Urinary symptoms — urgency, frequency, incomplete bladder emptying — from visceral hypersensitivity affecting bladder and pelvic floor; present in 50% of IBS patients
Dyspareunia (painful intercourse) — from visceral hypersensitivity and pelvic floor dysfunction; predominantly in women
Heartburn and acid reflux — GERD frequently overlaps with IBS (up to 30%); both functional GI disorders
Poor sleep — difficulty initiating sleep from pain anxiety; nocturnal awakening (though nocturnal BOWEL symptoms are unusual and warrant investigation)
Anxiety and low mood — highly prevalent comorbidities; worsened by chronic symptom burden and social restriction
Fibromyalgia and chronic pain — common comorbidity; shared central sensitisation mechanisms

extraintestinal_features.description: IBS is associated with numerous extraintestinal symptoms reflecting its systemic nature as a disorder of the pain-processing nervous system — not purely a bowel condition.

alarm_features_red_flags.description: These features in a patient with GI symptoms should PROMPT INVESTIGATION rather than empirical IBS management. They suggest possible organic disease (IBD, colorectal cancer, coeliac disease, etc.).
flags: Rectal bleeding or blood mixed with stool
New onset after age 50 years without prior bowel symptoms
Family history of colorectal cancer, IBD, or coeliac disease (in first-degree relative)
Nocturnal symptoms — pain or diarrhoea consistently waking from sleep
Short history with rapidly progressive symptoms (weeks, not months)
Fever (suggesting infective, inflammatory, or malignant cause)
Elevated inflammatory markers (raised CRP, ESR, elevated calprotectin)

key_points: IBS is common in children and adolescents — onset often during school age or puberty
Recurrent abdominal pain affecting school attendance is a very common presentation (school refusal from IBS must be distinguished from anxiety-based school avoidance)
Rome IV Paediatric Criteria for IBS: abdominal pain at least 4 days/month for at least 2 months, with criteria similar to adult Rome IV
Children may report headache, nausea, and fatigue more prominently than bowel symptoms
Parental anxiety about symptoms may amplify children's symptoms — family therapy approach often needed
Psychosocial stressors (school bullying, exams, family disruption) are important triggers in children
Management: education, reassurance, dietary modification, psychological support — minimise medicalisation in children

diagnostic_approach.philosophy: IBS should be diagnosed POSITIVELY on clinical grounds using Rome IV criteria after confirming absence of alarm features — NOT as a diagnosis of exclusion. Excessive investigation in every IBS patient is expensive, generates anxiety, and creates false positives without improving outcomes. NICE (UK 2017) recommends limited targeted investigations rather than extensive exclusion.
conditionally_required: Stool calprotectin — if any suspicion of IBD; especially if diarrhoea and raised CRP
Colonoscopy — if alarm features present; age >50; new onset; abnormal tests
diagnostic_approach.not_routinely_required: Abdominal imaging (CT/MRI), endoscopy, hydrogen breath tests, allergy panels, comprehensive stool panels — in uncomplicated IBS without alarm features

medical_history: Detailed symptom characterisation: onset, duration, frequency, location, quality of pain; relationship to defecation; stool frequency and consistency (BSFS type); urgency; straining; mucus
Subtyping: predominant bowel habit (constipation, diarrhoea, mixed, unsubtyped) — using stool diary over 2 weeks
Symptom timeline: onset after gastroenteritis (PI-IBS), after antibiotics, gradual onset; lifelong pattern vs recent change
Alarm feature screening: blood PR, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, family history colorectal cancer/IBD/coeliac
Trigger identification: dietary triggers (FODMAPs, lactose, gluten, fat, caffeine); stress; menstruation; travel; specific foods
Dietary history: FODMAP intake; fibre intake; hydration; meal regularity; eating behaviours
Psychological assessment: anxiety, depression, stress levels; major life events; childhood trauma or abuse history
Medication history: NSAIDs (worsen gut permeability), antibiotics (dysbiosis), PPIs, opioids (constipation), SSRIs, metformin (diarrhoea)
Family history: IBS (genetic component), inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, colorectal cancer
Impact assessment: work, social life, sleep, relationships — helps gauge severity and directs treatment intensity
physical_examination: General appearance: assess for weight loss, anaemia (pallor), nutritional status
Vital signs: temperature (fever excludes IBS — suggests organic disease), weight

Abdominal examination: inspection (distension, visible peristalsis), auscultation (bowel sounds — typically normal in IBS), percussion (tympany from gas), palpation (tenderness — usually mild diffuse tenderness on deep palpation; no guarding, rigidity, or peritonism which would suggest organic disease; palpable colon — especially left iliac fossa sigmoid colon may be tender)
Specific areas: RUQ (liver, gallbladder — excluded as cause); epigastrium (excluded peptic disease); suprapubic (bladder, uterus); umbilical; left iliac fossa (typically tender in IBS-D — sigmoid)
Palpation for masses: lymph nodes, abdominal mass (would prompt urgent investigation for cancer)
Anorectal examination (if constipation prominent): assess for anorectal structural abnormalities, rectal tone, prolapse, fissure
Pelvic examination in women (if pelvic pain prominent): assess for endometriosis, ovarian pathology, pelvic floor dysfunction
General: thyroid (exclude thyroid disease causing bowel symptoms), skin (Dermatitis herpetiformis — coeliac)

diagnostic_tests.description: Mandatory first-line investigation for ALL patients with GI symptoms. Iron-deficiency anaemia (low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin) is an alarm feature requiring urgent colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer or IBD. Eosinophilia may suggest eosinophilic gastroenteritis or parasitic infection. Leucocytosis suggests infection or inflammation.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for iron-deficiency anaemia (alarm feature); detect infection or inflammation; baseline assessment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hb <120 g/L (women) or <130 g/L (men) + low MCV + low ferritin = iron deficiency anaemia = alarm feature; MCV >100 = macrocytic (B12/folate deficiency — associated with coeliac); eosinophilia: >0.4 × 10⁹/L

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Coeliac Serology (Tissue Transglutaminase IgA — TTG IgA + Total IgA)
diagnostic_tests.description: MANDATORY in all patients with IBS-D or IBS-M symptoms. Coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) frequently presents with diarrhoea, bloating, and abdominal pain — clinically identical to IBS-D. Prevalence of coeliac in patients with IBS-like symptoms: 4x higher than general population. Total IgA must also be measured because IgA deficiency (1 in 300) gives a false-negative TTG IgA — if IgA deficient, use TTG IgG or deamidated gliadin antibodies (DGP).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude coeliac disease — MANDATORY in IBS-D and IBS-M; also check in IBS-C with unexplained symptoms
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TTG IgA >10 U/mL (or >3x ULN): positive — requires confirmatory duodenal biopsy; Total IgA <0.07 g/L: IgA deficient — use TTG IgG instead

diagnostic_tests.test_name: C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated CRP and ESR suggest organic inflammatory disease (IBD, infection, malignancy) rather than IBS. CRP is normal (<5 mg/L) in uncomplicated IBS in the vast majority of patients. Elevated CRP in a patient with diarrhoea and abdominal pain → prioritise investigation for IBD.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude inflammatory organic disease (IBD, malignancy, infection); support IBS diagnosis when normal
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CRP >5 mg/L with IBS symptoms: consider IBD or other organic disease — calprotectin and colonoscopy

diagnostic_tests.description: Hyperthyroidism causes diarrhoea, weight loss, and abdominal discomfort — mimicking IBS-D. Hypothyroidism causes constipation, bloating, and fatigue — mimicking IBS-C. TSH screening should be performed at initial IBS assessment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude thyroid disease as cause of GI symptoms; mandatory in initial workup
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TSH <0.4 mIU/L: hyperthyroidism (IBS-D mimic); TSH >4 mIU/L: hypothyroidism (IBS-C mimic)

diagnostic_tests.description: Calprotectin is a protein released by neutrophils — elevated in intestinal inflammation (IBD, colorectal cancer, infection). A crucial test to DISTINGUISH IBS from inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's/UC). In uncomplicated IBS: calprotectin is typically normal (<50 µg/g). Elevated calprotectin (>200 µg/g) in a patient with IBS-like symptoms strongly suggests IBD and warrants colonoscopy.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Distinguish IBS from IBD (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis); screen for intestinal inflammation; support positive IBS diagnosis when normal
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: <50 µg/g: low risk of IBD (IBS diagnosis supported); 50-200 µg/g: borderline (repeat or further investigation); >200 µg/g: high risk of IBD — urgent colonoscopy
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity_specificity: Sensitivity for IBD ~93%; Specificity ~96% (cut-off 50 µg/g) — excellent test for IBD exclusion

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Stool Culture and Ova, Cysts and Parasites (OCP)
diagnostic_tests.description: Stool culture for bacterial pathogens (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia, E. coli O157:H7) and OCP examination for parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba). Indicated when: acute onset diarrhoea, recent travel to endemic areas, history of gastroenteritis preceding IBS, or atypical IBS-D features.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude infective cause of diarrhoea; diagnose PI-IBS precipitant; detect Giardia (common chronic IBS-D mimic); mandatory in returned travellers
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive Giardia antigen or trophozoites: treat with metronidazole (may resolve IBS-D symptoms completely if Giardia-driven)

diagnostic_tests.description: Tests for: (1) Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO): lactulose or glucose hydrogen breath test — excess hydrogen (>20 ppm rise above baseline within 90 min) suggests SIBO; methane >10 ppm on any reading suggests methane-dominant SIBO (associated with constipation). (2) Lactose intolerance: 50g lactose hydrogen breath test. (3) Fructose malabsorption: 25g fructose hydrogen breath test.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose SIBO (significant subset of IBS-D and IBS-C); confirm lactose intolerance; confirm fructose malabsorption
diagnostic_tests.clinical_relevance: SIBO diagnosis allows targeted rifaximin treatment; lactose and fructose malabsorption confirms need for dietary restriction
diagnostic_tests.limitation: High false-positive rates with lactulose test; glucose test more specific for SIBO but misses distal SIBO; interpretation requires expertise

diagnostic_tests.description: Not indicated in all IBS patients — reserved for those with alarm features or specific indications. Allows direct visualisation of colorectal mucosa, detection of IBD (Crohn's or UC — may have normal macroscopic appearance but microscopic colitis on biopsy), colorectal polyps and cancer, diverticular disease, and ischaemic colitis.
indications: Alarm features (rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia)
Failure to respond to IBS treatment
Microscopic colitis suspected (chronic watery diarrhoea in older women — NOT IBD macroscopically but biopsies show collagenous or lymphocytic colitis)
diagnostic_tests.microscopic_colitis: Colonoscopy APPEARS NORMAL in microscopic colitis — diagnosis requires biopsies; presents identically to IBS-D in older patients; treat with budesonide

diagnostic_tests.test_name: SeHCAT Test (75-Selenium Homocholic Acid Taurine) — Bile Acid Malabsorption
diagnostic_tests.description: Most accurate test for bile acid malabsorption (BAM) — measures retention of a radiolabelled bile acid over 7 days. <15% retention: severe BAM; 15-25%: moderate; >25%: normal. BAM is a critical diagnosis to make in IBS-D patients — it responds dramatically to bile acid sequestrants and does NOT respond to typical IBS treatments. Treat if 7-day retention <15% (severe BAM).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose bile acid malabsorption in IBS-D patients; guide use of bile acid sequestrants
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: 7-day retention <10%: severe BAM (90% treatment response to cholestyramine); 10-15%: moderate; >25%: normal
diagnostic_tests.alternative: Fasting serum 7alphaC4 (7α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one) — elevated in BAM; easier but less specific than SeHCAT

diagnostic_tests.description: A validated 5-item patient-reported questionnaire scoring: abdominal pain severity (0-100), abdominal pain frequency (0-100), bloating (0-100), bowel habit dissatisfaction (0-100), and life interference (0-100). Total score: 0-500. Used to quantify symptom severity, classify disease severity, and monitor treatment response.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Quantify IBS severity; monitor treatment response; guide treatment escalation decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Score <75: in remission; 75-175: mild; 175-300: moderate; >300: severe. A decrease of ≥50 points = clinically meaningful improvement
diagnostic_tests.clinical_use: Baseline and at 4-8 weeks after treatment changes; allows objective monitoring without invasive tests

diagnostic_tests.description: Patient records daily: stool frequency, BSFS type (1-7), presence of urgency, completeness of evacuation, bloating severity (0-10), pain severity (0-10), foods eaten, stress level, and medications. Essential for IBS subtyping (IBS-C vs IBS-D vs IBS-M), identifying dietary triggers, and guiding low FODMAP diet decisions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Accurate IBS subtyping; identify dietary and lifestyle triggers; monitor response to interventions; essential before starting low FODMAP elimination phase

diagnostic_tests.description: For patients with severe refractory IBS-C and prominent straining/incomplete evacuation — anorectal manometry (measures sphincter pressures and rectoanal coordination) and defecating proctogram (dynamic imaging of defecation) identify pelvic floor dyssynergia (paradoxical anal sphincter contraction during straining — prevents effective evacuation). Pelvic floor physiotherapy is highly effective for dyssynergia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose pelvic floor dyssynergia in refractory IBS-C; guide biofeedback therapy for pelvic floor rehabilitation
diagnostic_tests.clinical_importance: Pelvic floor dyssynergia affects 25-30% of patients with severe IBS-C — biofeedback is >75% effective for this condition

medicines.note: IBS pharmacotherapy is directed by subtype (IBS-C vs IBS-D vs IBS-M) and symptom predominance. No single drug treats all IBS symptoms. Lifestyle modification and dietary intervention (low FODMAP) remain the foundation — medications are adjuncts. All medications require prescription from a licensed physician or gastroenterologist. Treatment should be individualised.
treatment_principles: Positive diagnosis and patient education is itself therapeutic — reducing diagnostic uncertainty significantly improves symptoms
Treat predominant symptom (pain, constipation, diarrhoea, bloating) and IBS subtype
Start with lifestyle measures and dietary interventions before pharmacotherapy
Step-up treatment based on symptom severity (mild → dietary/lifestyle; moderate → first-line drugs; severe → neuromodulators + psychology)
Reassess response at 4-8 weeks; switch drugs if insufficient response after 12 weeks
Long-term drug use review — IBS is chronic; avoid unnecessary long-term medication; use lowest effective dose

categories.category_name: Antispasmodics (First-Line for Abdominal Pain and Cramping)
categories.purpose: Reduce intestinal smooth muscle spasm — the cause of cramping pain in IBS. Effective for acute pain relief and reducing post-prandial cramping. Recommended as first-line symptomatic treatment for abdominal pain by NICE (UK) and ACG (USA) guidelines.

medicines.name: Mebeverine
medicines.dosage: 135mg three times daily 20 minutes before meals (standard tablets); 200mg twice daily (modified-release capsules)
medicines.use_case: First-line antispasmodic for IBS abdominal pain and cramping — ALL subtypes; PRN or regular dosing; widely used and well-tolerated; NICE first-line recommendation
medicines.mechanism: Direct smooth muscle relaxant (not anticholinergic); acts on musculotropic sites in intestinal smooth muscle; does not cause systemic anticholinergic side effects
side_effects: Minimal — one of the safest antispasmodics
medicines.advantage: No anticholinergic side effects (unlike hyoscine); safe in elderly, BPH, glaucoma, pregnancy (limited data)

medicines.name: Hyoscine Butylbromide (Buscopan)
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg three to four times daily PRN or regularly; maximum 80mg/day oral
medicines.use_case: Acute IBS abdominal cramping pain (PRN use); also used for other causes of spasmodic abdominal pain (renal colic, biliary colic); rapid onset of effect
medicines.mechanism: Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) — blocks M3 muscarinic receptors in intestinal smooth muscle causing relaxation; poor systemic absorption after oral dosing (quaternary ammonium compound)
side_effects: Minimal with oral formulation due to poor absorption
IV use: dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision (anticholinergic)
medicines.note: IV/IM buscopan provides faster relief for severe acute abdominal cramping

medicines.name: Dicyclomine (Dicycloverine)
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg three times daily
medicines.use_case: Antispasmodic for IBS pain; widely available in India; both direct smooth muscle relaxant and anticholinergic properties

medicines.name: Peppermint Oil (Enteric-Coated Capsules)
medicines.dosage: 0.2-0.4mL peppermint oil (1-2 capsules) three times daily 30-60 minutes BEFORE meals; enteric-coated releases in small intestine/colon (not stomach)
medicines.use_case: IBS abdominal pain and cramping; bloating and gas; recommended by ACG, NICE, and BSG as first-line antispasmodic; significant meta-analysis evidence
medicines.mechanism: L-menthol in peppermint oil — blocks calcium channels in intestinal smooth muscle → relaxes smooth muscle (calcium channel antagonist in gut); reduces visceral hypersensitivity (TRPM8 receptor agonist — counter-irritant on pain nerves); reduces TRPV1 pain receptor activation
side_effects: Heartburn and acid reflux (from LES relaxation — must use ENTERIC-COATED to prevent this)
medicines.evidence: Meta-analysis (Ford 2014): peppermint oil significantly superior to placebo for global IBS symptoms and abdominal pain (NNT = 5); ACG Guidelines 2021: conditional recommendation
medicines.critical_note: MUST use enteric-coated capsules — plain peppermint oil or peppermint tea WORSENS heartburn and is NOT equivalent

categories.purpose: Reduce stool frequency, improve stool consistency, and reduce urgency in IBS-D. Symptomatic relief only — do not treat the underlying disorder.

medicines.name: Loperamide
medicines.dosage: 2-4mg before anticipated diarrhoea episodes or after each loose stool; maximum 16mg/day; can take prophylactically before meals, social events, or travel
medicines.use_case: IBS-D — most commonly used antidiarrhoeal for IBS; reduces stool frequency, improves stool consistency, reduces urgency; prophylactic use before social events, meals, or travel for symptom control
medicines.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor agonist in the gut (does not cross blood-brain barrier — no CNS effects at therapeutic doses); reduces intestinal motility and secretion; increases anal sphincter tone (reduces urgency incontinence risk)
contraindications: Inflammatory bowel disease (may cause toxic megacolon)
medicines.clinical_tip: Start with 2mg before a known trigger (meal, social event) — can increase to 4mg; use PRN or regular depending on symptom pattern; not for use in acute infectious diarrhoea

categories.purpose: Target colonic and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth without systemic antibiotic effects. Rifaximin is the only antibiotic with robust Phase 3 RCT evidence for IBS without constipation.

medicines.name: Rifaximin
medicines.dosage: IBS-D (non-constipated IBS): 550mg three times daily for 14 days; SIBO: 400-550mg three times daily for 14 days; may be repeated every 3-6 months for relapse
medicines.use_case: Non-constipated IBS (IBS-D, IBS-M) with bloating — FDA approved for IBS-D; SIBO treatment; significant bloating and flatulence
medicines.mechanism: Non-absorbable rifamycin antibiotic — acts entirely within the GI lumen; broad spectrum against gram-positive and gram-negative gut bacteria; reduces bacterial overgrowth and fermentation without systemic antibiotic effects; reduces luminal LPS; modifies gut microbiome favourably
medicines.evidence: TARGET 1 and TARGET 2 Phase 3 trials: rifaximin 550mg TDS × 14 days achieved adequate relief of global IBS symptoms in 40% vs 31% placebo; sustained response up to 10 weeks after completing treatment course
side_effects: C. difficile infection risk very low (unlike systemic antibiotics)
medicines.advantage: Non-absorbable → no systemic antibiotic side effects; no resistance to systemic antibiotics; can be repeated safely; unique in being the only antibiotic with proven IBS efficacy

categories.purpose: Increase intestinal fluid secretion and/or accelerate colonic transit, improving stool frequency and consistency in IBS-C. More effective than laxatives as they also reduce abdominal pain (distinguishing from simple constipation treatment).

medicines.name: Linaclotide
medicines.dosage: IBS-C: 290mcg once daily at least 30-60 min before breakfast; Chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC): 145mcg once daily
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for moderate-severe IBS-C — FDA and EMA approved for IBS-C; reduces both constipation AND abdominal pain (unique — laxatives don't reduce pain); approved for adults ≥18
medicines.mechanism: Guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C) receptor agonist in intestinal epithelial cells → increases intracellular cGMP → activates CFTR chloride channel → chloride and water secretion into intestinal lumen (improves stool consistency); also reduces visceral pain signals via CGMP activation of visceral nociceptors (pain-reducing mechanism independent of stool improvement)
side_effects: Diarrhoea (most common and dose-limiting — up to 20%; manage by dose reduction; take 30-60 min before breakfast to limit post-breakfast diarrhoea)
contraindications: Children under 6 years (risk of dehydration; FDA black box warning)
medicines.clinical_tip: Take at least 30-60 minutes BEFORE breakfast (taking on empty stomach reduces transit time allowing drug to act distally before meal-stimulated motility); if diarrhoea problematic, try 145mcg dose

medicines.name: Plecanatide
medicines.dosage: 3mg once daily with or without food
medicines.use_case: IBS-C and chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC) — FDA approved 2017; similar mechanism to linaclotide; may be better tolerated (less diarrhoea than linaclotide)
medicines.mechanism: GC-C receptor agonist (similar to linaclotide but more selective for acidic GC-C receptor isoform — may account for improved tolerability); increases intestinal fluid secretion; reduces visceral pain

medicines.name: Lubiprostone
medicines.dosage: IBS-C (women): 8mcg twice daily with food; Chronic idiopathic constipation: 24mcg twice daily
medicines.use_case: IBS-C in women aged 18 and over — FDA approved; also for CIC and opioid-induced constipation; approved specifically in women (clinical trials predominantly in women)
medicines.mechanism: Chloride channel (ClC-2) activator on intestinal epithelial apical surface → chloride and water secretion into intestinal lumen → softens stool and accelerates transit; also stimulates mucus secretion

medicines.name: Prucalopride
medicines.dosage: 2mg once daily (1mg in elderly ≥65 years); evaluate at 4 weeks
medicines.use_case: Chronic constipation and IBS-C not responding to laxatives; highly selective 5-HT4 agonist; most evidence in chronic constipation but used for IBS-C; accelerates colonic transit
medicines.mechanism: Highly selective 5-HT4 receptor agonist in enteric nervous system → promotes high-amplitude propagating contractions (HAPCs) in colon → accelerated colonic transit
medicines.advantage: High selectivity for 5-HT4 (vs tegaserod which had cardiac concerns) — excellent cardiac safety profile in large clinical trials

medicines.name: Tenapanor
medicines.dosage: 50mg twice daily immediately before breakfast and dinner
medicines.use_case: IBS-C — FDA approved 2019; novel mechanism; reduces abdominal pain AND improves constipation
medicines.mechanism: NHE3 (sodium-hydrogen exchanger 3) inhibitor in intestinal epithelium → reduces sodium absorption in gut → increases intraluminal water → softer stools and faster transit; also reduces paracellular phosphate absorption (approved for hyperphosphataemia in CKD); reduces visceral hypersensitivity via reduced intracellular pH changes

categories.purpose: Draw water into the intestinal lumen via osmosis, softening stools and increasing bowel frequency. Generally recommended as second-line after secretagogues in IBS-C (laxatives reduce constipation but typically do NOT reduce abdominal pain — a key IBS-C feature).
categories.note: Laxatives treat constipation symptoms but do NOT address visceral pain — if pain is the dominant symptom in IBS-C, secretagogues (linaclotide) or antispasmodics are preferred.

medicines.name: Polyethylene Glycol / Macrogol
medicines.form: Oral powder sachet dissolved in water
medicines.dosage: 1-3 sachets daily dissolved in water; titrate to achieve 1-2 soft stools daily
medicines.use_case: IBS-C — relieves constipation; well-tolerated; can be used long-term; may be used alongside antispasmodics for combined pain and constipation treatment
medicines.mechanism: Osmotic agent — non-absorbable PEG polymer attracts and holds water in intestinal lumen by osmosis → increases stool water content and weight → promotes defecation
medicines.advantage: Effective, safe, available OTC; long-term use acceptable; preferred over lactulose (less fermentation/gas)

medicines.name: Lactulose
medicines.dosage: 15-45mL once or twice daily; adjust to effect; 1-3 days for full effect
medicines.use_case: IBS-C — mild to moderate constipation; widely available and inexpensive in India; also used for hepatic encephalopathy at higher doses
medicines.mechanism: Non-absorbable disaccharide — osmotic laxative + colonic bacterial fermentation (to lactate and acetate → acidifies colon → promotes colonic motility)
side_effects: Bloating and flatulence — SIGNIFICANT (from fermentation); may worsen bloating in IBS
medicines.note: Fermentation causes significant gas — may worsen bloating in IBS patients; macrogol (Movicol) preferred for IBS-C due to less bloating

categories.purpose: Block serotonin 5-HT3 receptors in the gut — the primary receptor mediating rapid gut transit, urgency, and pain signalling in IBS-D. Highly effective for severe IBS-D especially when urgency incontinence is present.

medicines.name: Alosetron
medicines.dosage: 0.5mg twice daily × 4 weeks; increase to 1mg twice daily if tolerated and insufficient response; discontinue if constipation or ischaemic colitis develops
medicines.use_case: Severe IBS-D in WOMEN — FDA approved (under Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy — REMS programme in USA) for women with severe IBS-D not responding to conventional therapy
medicines.mechanism: Selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist — reduces colonic transit, reduces visceral hypersensitivity, reduces urgency, reduces stool frequency; most effective 5-HT3 antagonist available
side_effects: Constipation (most common — dose-limiting; discontinue if severe constipation or impaction)
ISCHAEMIC COLITIS (rare but potentially serious — 0.15 per 1000 patient-years; abdominal pain + bloody diarrhoea = stop immediately; rectal ischaemia)
medicines.availability: USA only (REMS programme); not available in UK, India, or most other countries; prescribers must be registered
medicines.black_box_warning: Ischaemic colitis and serious complications of constipation; prescribe only to women with severe IBS-D not responding to conventional therapy

medicines.name: Ondansetron (Off-Label IBS-D)
medicines.dosage: 4-8mg once daily or twice daily (off-label for IBS-D); start with 4mg and titrate
medicines.use_case: Off-label use for IBS-D — rapidly growing evidence base; UK TARDIS trial showed significant improvement in stool consistency, urgency, and frequency without serious side effects; widely used 'off-label' in UK gastroenterology for IBS-D; safe, inexpensive, widely available
medicines.mechanism: 5-HT3 receptor antagonist — reduces colonic transit and urgency; same mechanism as alosetron but less potent and with much better safety profile
medicines.evidence: TARDIS trial (Garsed et al. 2014): ondansetron 4-16mg/day significantly improved stool consistency (BSFS), urgency, and pain in IBS-D vs placebo; good safety profile
side_effects: QT prolongation (at high doses — ECG monitoring in cardiac patients)
medicines.note: Not formally approved for IBS in any country but widely recommended off-label; safe alternative to alosetron without REMS requirements

categories.category_name: Bile Acid Sequestrants (IBS-D with Bile Acid Malabsorption)
categories.purpose: Bind bile acids in the intestine preventing them from reaching the colon where they cause secretory diarrhoea. Highly effective (80-90% response) when bile acid malabsorption (BAM) is the underlying cause of IBS-D.

medicines.name: Cholestyramine
medicines.dosage: 4g once to four times daily (titrate to response); start with 4g once daily and increase
medicines.use_case: Bile acid malabsorption (BAM) — first-line treatment; effective in 70-90% of patients with BAM on SeHCAT testing; also useful for post-cholecystectomy diarrhoea and Crohn's ileitis
medicines.mechanism: Non-absorbable anion-exchange resin — binds bile acids in intestinal lumen preventing colonic entry; reduces bile acid-induced colonic secretion and accelerated transit
side_effects: Reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) with long-term use — supplement vitamins
Drug interactions: binds many drugs — separate all medications by at least 1-4 hours
medicines.note: Take cholestyramine at least 1-4 hours apart from other medications (adsorbs drugs)

medicines.name: Colesevelam
medicines.dosage: 625mg three to six tablets daily (divided doses with meals)
medicines.use_case: BAM — better tolerated than cholestyramine (tablet formulation, fewer GI side effects); also approved for hypercholesterolaemia and type 2 diabetes
medicines.advantage: Better tolerated than cholestyramine; tablet formulation (not powder); fewer drug interactions

categories.purpose: At low doses (below antidepressant doses), TCAs exert central and peripheral pain-modulating effects on the gut-brain axis — reducing visceral hypersensitivity, slowing intestinal transit, and improving sleep. MOST EFFECTIVE pharmacotherapy for abdominal pain in IBS. Recommended by ACG (American College of Gastroenterology) 2021 guidelines as a strong recommendation for global IBS symptoms.
categories.note: Explain clearly to patients: TCAs for IBS are prescribed at MUCH LOWER doses than for depression — they are being used as pain modulators, not antidepressants. Addressing this misunderstanding upfront is crucial for treatment adherence.

medicines.name: Amitriptyline
medicines.dosage: Starting: 10mg once daily at night; increase by 10mg every 2-4 weeks; usual therapeutic range for IBS: 25-75mg at night; maximum 150mg (antidepressant dose — rarely needed for IBS)
medicines.use_case: IBS abdominal pain (all subtypes, particularly IBS-D where slowing of transit is beneficial); IBS with insomnia (sedating — take at night); IBS with comorbid depression/anxiety; IBS with visceral hypersensitivity; considered first-choice neuromodulator for IBS by multiple guidelines
medicines.mechanism: Multiple mechanisms: reduces NMDA receptor-mediated central sensitisation (visceral hypersensitivity); reduces ascending pain signalling to thalamus and cortex; slows intestinal transit (anticholinergic — beneficial in IBS-D); improves sleep architecture; mild 5-HT/noradrenaline reuptake inhibition at higher doses
side_effects: Drowsiness/sedation — take at night (can be beneficial for sleep)
QT prolongation (check ECG at baseline in cardiac patients)
medicines.monitoring: Baseline ECG; blood pressure; review at 4-8 weeks; if no benefit by 12 weeks at adequate dose — consider alternative neuromodulator
medicines.ibs_diarrhoea_benefit: Anticholinergic slowing of gut motility is BENEFICIAL in IBS-D (reduces urgency and frequency)

medicines.name: Nortriptyline
medicines.dosage: 10-75mg at night
medicines.use_case: IBS abdominal pain; alternative to amitriptyline with fewer anticholinergic side effects and less sedation; better tolerated in elderly
medicines.side_effects: Fewer anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline; less sedation; preferred in elderly patients

categories.category_name: Low-Dose SSRIs and SNRIs (IBS with Comorbid Anxiety or Depression)
categories.purpose: SSRIs and SNRIs at low doses reduce central sensitisation and visceral hypersensitivity while treating comorbid anxiety and depression. SSRIs tend to accelerate gut transit (beneficial in IBS-C; may worsen IBS-D). ACG 2021: conditional recommendation for SSRIs for global IBS symptoms.
categories.note: SSRIs are particularly preferred in IBS-C (accelerate transit) and when significant comorbid anxiety or depression is present. TCAs preferred for IBS-D (slow transit beneficial).

medicines.name: Fluoxetine
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg once daily (lower than antidepressant dose of 20-60mg; start 10mg in IBS)
medicines.use_case: IBS with predominant constipation (IBS-C) — accelerates gut transit; IBS with comorbid depression or anxiety; IBS with somatic symptom disorder
medicines.mechanism: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor — increases synaptic 5-HT; central visceral pain modulation; accelerates gut transit (5-HT in gut promotes motility — beneficial in IBS-C)

medicines.name: Citalopram / Escitalopram
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg once daily (start low)
medicines.use_case: IBS with comorbid anxiety or depression; IBS-C (transit acceleration); better GI tolerability than fluoxetine; escitalopram preferred (fewer drug interactions)

medicines.name: Duloxetine
medicines.dosage: 30-60mg once daily (start 30mg for IBS)
medicines.use_case: IBS with comorbid fibromyalgia or chronic pain (SNRI particularly effective for central sensitisation syndromes); IBS with anxiety and depression; painful IBS
medicines.mechanism: SNRI — noradrenaline reuptake inhibition provides additional pain modulation (descending inhibitory pathway activation) vs SSRIs alone; central sensitisation reduction

categories.purpose: Modulate the gut microbiome, reduce intestinal permeability, reduce mucosal immune activation, and alter gut-brain signalling. Meta-analyses support probiotic use in IBS for overall symptom improvement, bloating reduction, and flatulence. Effects are strain-specific — different probiotic species and strains have different effects.
categories.note: Probiotics generally have good safety profiles. Effects are modest and variable — some patients respond well; others do not. Trial for 4-8 weeks and continue if beneficial. Strain-specific effects are important.

medicines.name: Bifidobacterium longum + Lactobacillus acidophilus + Multiple Strain Combinations
medicines.dosage: Follow product instructions; typically 1-2 capsules or sachets daily; trial for 4-8 weeks
medicines.use_case: IBS global symptom improvement; bloating and gas reduction; flatulence; PI-IBS (microbiome restoration); IBS during and after antibiotic treatment
medicines.mechanism: Colonise intestinal epithelium competitively; reduce pathogenic bacteria; produce SCFAs (butyrate seals tight junctions); modulate mucosal immune response; communicate with enteric nervous system via vagal signalling; produce GABA and serotonin precursors
medicines.evidence: Cochrane meta-analysis (Ford 2014): probiotics significantly better than placebo for IBS global symptoms (RR 0.79; NNT=7) and bloating; Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 has strongest evidence for pain, bloating, and bowel habits in IBS; VSL#3 specific evidence for bloating
side_effects: Transient increased gas and bloating (first 1-2 weeks as microbiome adjusts)
Avoid in severely immunocompromised patients (theoretical bacteraemia risk — extremely rare)
medicines.best_strains_for_ibs: Bifidobacterium longum 35624 (Align/Alflorex); Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG; VSL#3 (multi-strain for bloating); Saccharomyces boulardii (IBS-D)

medicines.name: Eluxadoline
medicines.dosage: 100mg twice daily with food; 75mg twice daily in patients without a gallbladder or with moderate hepatic impairment
medicines.use_case: IBS-D — FDA approved; reduces diarrhoea and abdominal pain through combined opioid receptor actions
medicines.mechanism: Mixed mu-opioid receptor agonist (reduces gut motility — reduces diarrhoea) / delta-opioid receptor antagonist (prevents constipation from pure mu-agonism) / kappa-opioid receptor agonist (local analgesic — reduces visceral pain)
side_effects: PANCREATITIS (risk — contraindicated without a gallbladder due to sphincter of Oddi dysfunction risk; avoid in patients with history of pancreatitis or biliary tract disease)

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is arguably the most important management strategy in IBS — up to 90% of IBS patients report that food triggers their symptoms, and dietary modification is the most impactful non-pharmacological intervention. The Low FODMAP Diet is the most evidence-based dietary intervention for IBS, with clinical trials demonstrating symptom improvement in 50-75% of patients. However, IBS dietary management is highly individualised — triggers vary significantly between patients, requiring a personalised approach ideally guided by a specialist GI dietitian.

low_fodmap_diet.description: The Low FODMAP Diet targets Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides And Polyols — short-chain carbohydrates that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine, fermented rapidly by colonic bacteria, producing gas and drawing water into the bowel, causing bloating, pain, and altered stool consistency.

what_are_fodmaps.Oligosaccharides: Fructans (wheat, rye, garlic, onion, leek) and Galacto-oligosaccharides/GOS (legumes, chickpeas, lentils, cashews)
what_are_fodmaps.Disaccharides: Lactose (milk, yoghurt, soft cheeses, ice cream)
what_are_fodmaps.Monosaccharides: Excess fructose (honey, apples, pears, mango, high-fructose corn syrup)
what_are_fodmaps.Polyols: Sorbitol (apples, pears, plums, apricots, diet products), Mannitol (mushrooms, cauliflower, diet products), Xylitol and other polyols in sugar-free products

phase_1_elimination.description: Strict elimination of ALL high-FODMAP foods simultaneously. This phase should be done under guidance of a registered dietitian (RD) with IBS experience — the diet is complex, restricts many nutritious foods, and risks nutritional deficiency if followed without professional guidance.
phase_1_elimination.goal: Achieve symptom improvement — in responders (50-75%), significant improvement typically occurs within 2-4 weeks

phase_2_reintroduction.description: Systematic reintroduction of individual FODMAP groups, one at a time, every 3-4 days. Each FODMAP type is tested separately to identify which FODMAP subgroups (not all) the individual patient is sensitive to. Not all patients react to all FODMAPs.
phase_2_reintroduction.goal: Identify PERSONAL triggers — individual threshold amounts for each FODMAP group

phase_3_personalisation.description: Based on reintroduction testing, create a personalised long-term diet that avoids only the specific FODMAPs and quantities that trigger symptoms in that individual — the most liberal diet possible while maintaining symptom control.
phase_3_personalisation.goal: Sustainable long-term diet with maximum nutritional diversity while controlling symptoms

low_fodmap_diet.evidence: Multiple RCTs (including Halmos 2014, Staudacher 2011, Bohn 2015): Low FODMAP diet improves global IBS symptoms in 50-75% of patients vs 20-30% on control diet; reduces bloating, pain, diarrhoea, urgency, and flatulence; NNT approximately 3-4
low_fodmap_diet.concerns: Long-term strict low FODMAP diet may reduce microbiome diversity (FODMAPs are prebiotic) — Phase 3 personalisation essential; not to be followed strictly indefinitely without Phase 2-3

recommended_foods.note: These vegetables are well tolerated by most IBS patients and should form the basis of vegetable intake

items.food: Courgette (Zucchini), Bell peppers, Carrots, Aubergine (Eggplant), Green beans, Cucumber, Lettuce, Spinach, Kale, Tomato (up to 1 medium), Olives
items.benefit: Low fermentable carbohydrate content; well-tolerated; rich in vitamins, minerals, antioxidants; provide dietary fibre without significant gas production

items.food: Potato, Sweet potato, Parsnip, Swede (Rutabaga)
items.benefit: Low FODMAP; filling; provide resistant starch (low-FODMAP amounts); vitamins; good energy source

items.food: Broccoli (small portions — up to 75g per meal), Cabbage (common — up to 75g), Celery (up to 1 stalk)
items.benefit: Nutritious; tolerated in limited portions (FODMAPs present but at sub-threshold amounts in small servings)
items.caution: PORTION-SENSITIVE — exceeding threshold amounts triggers symptoms; introduce carefully

items.food: Blueberries, Strawberries, Raspberries, Oranges, Mandarins, Kiwi, Grapes, Pineapple, Melon (cantaloupe, honeydew — small portion)
items.benefit: Well-tolerated in normal portion sizes; antioxidants; vitamins; fibre; anti-inflammatory

items.food: Bananas (just ripe — not over-ripe; firm yellow with no brown spots), Papaya
items.benefit: Ripe bananas are low FODMAP; potassium; gentle on gut; anti-IBS nutritional profile
items.caution: RIPE bananas only — unripe green bananas are low FODMAP; over-ripe bananas have higher fructose content

items.food: Lean meats and poultry: Chicken, Turkey, Beef, Lamb, Pork (unprocessed, plain)
items.benefit: Zero FODMAP; complete protein; essential amino acids; iron; B12; safe for IBS

items.food: Fish and seafood (fresh, not marinated or breaded with FODMAP ingredients)
items.benefit: Zero FODMAP; omega-3 anti-inflammatory; high-quality protein; safe for IBS

items.food: Eggs
items.benefit: Zero FODMAP; complete protein; all essential amino acids; versatile; safe for IBS

items.food: Firm tofu, Tempeh (in limited amounts)
items.benefit: Low FODMAP (FIRM tofu — water content reduced; soft tofu is higher FODMAP); plant protein; good for vegetarian IBS patients
items.caution: Firm/extra-firm tofu only; soft or silken tofu has higher GOS content

items.food: Tinned chickpeas (drained and rinsed — up to ¼ cup), Tinned lentils (drained and rinsed — ½ cup)
items.benefit: Canning and rinsing leaches FODMAPs into brine — drained and rinsed portions can be low FODMAP in small amounts; plant protein and fibre for IBS patients who are vegetarian
items.caution: Portion-critical — exceeding amounts triggers symptoms; do NOT use dried and cooked legumes (higher FODMAP)

items.food: White rice, Brown rice, Quinoa, Oats (uncontaminated/gluten-free oats), Polenta, Buckwheat, Millet
items.benefit: Low FODMAP; these grains do NOT contain fructans (unlike wheat and rye); generally well tolerated; provide energy and B vitamins

items.food: Sourdough spelt bread or sourdough wheat bread (long-fermented — certain types)
items.benefit: Long fermentation of sourdough (>12 hours) degrades fructans in wheat flour — some IBS patients tolerate small amounts of traditional sourdough bread; portion-dependent
items.caution: Individual response variable; start with small amount (1 slice); commercial 'sourdough' bread is often not genuinely long-fermented

items.food: Gluten-free bread, pasta, crackers (made from rice, corn, or potato flours)
items.benefit: FODMAP-free; safe for IBS patients with fructan sensitivity (wheat intolerance in IBS is from fructans, not gluten); practical alternative to wheat-based products
items.note: Check ingredients — some GF products contain high-FODMAP ingredients (honey, apple juice, chicory root/inulin, FOS, xylitol)

items.food: Lactose-free milk, Lactose-free yogurt, Hard aged cheeses (cheddar, parmesan, brie, camembert — naturally low lactose)
items.benefit: Well-tolerated dairy alternatives or low-lactose dairy; calcium; protein; vitamin D; important for bone health in IBS patients who restrict dairy

items.food: Almond milk (no added inulin), Rice milk, Oat milk (limited — moderate FODMAP)
items.benefit: Dairy-free alternatives; useful if lactose is a trigger; almond milk is low FODMAP in 250mL serving
items.caution: READ LABELS — many plant milks contain added chicory root, inulin, or FOS (high FODMAP)

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — soluble fibre specifically (NOT insoluble bran) is recommended for IBS-C; forms a gel that softens stools and moderates gut transit without excessive fermentation

items.food: Psyllium husk (ispaghula) — Plantago ovata
items.benefit: MOST EVIDENCE for IBS: soluble fibre that forms a gel; reduces constipation (IBS-C); paradoxically also reduces diarrhoea by adsorbing excess water; reduces pain and bloating more than insoluble bran; meta-analysis: NNT=6 for IBS symptom improvement
items.dosage: Start 5g (1 teaspoon) once daily in 300mL water; increase to 10-20g/day over 2-4 weeks; ESSENTIAL to take with large amount of water (2+ glasses — risk of oesophageal obstruction if insufficient water)
items.frequency: Once or twice daily — take with large amount of water

items.food: Oats (beta-glucan)
items.benefit: Soluble fibre; beta-glucan moderates gut transit; reduces cholesterol; anti-inflammatory; gentle for IBS; well tolerated

items.food: Ginger tea (fresh ginger root)
items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory (6-gingerol, 6-shogaol); antispasmodic (relaxes intestinal smooth muscle); anti-nausea; promotes gastric emptying; reduces bloating; helpful for IBS-D and IBS nausea
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily; fresh ginger (1-2cm) steeped in hot water

items.food: Peppermint tea (not for those with GERD)
items.benefit: Menthol relaxes intestinal smooth muscle — antispasmodic; reduces bloating and cramping; beneficial for IBS
items.caution: Avoid with GERD — peppermint relaxes LES; prefer peppermint OIL CAPSULES (enteric-coated) which deliver to bowel not stomach

items.food: Bone broth (chicken or vegetable — plain, without high-FODMAP additions)
items.benefit: Gelatine (glycine) supports intestinal epithelial integrity; reduces intestinal permeability ('leaky gut'); gut-healing; easily digestible; hydrating
items.frequency: Daily as a warm drink or soup base

items.food: Turmeric (curcumin)
items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory (NF-κB inhibition); reduces mucosal immune activation in IBS; some trial evidence for symptom improvement; anti-spasmodic properties; small RCT: curcumin supplementation reduced IBS symptom severity
items.frequency: Daily in cooking or supplement (500-1000mg curcumin with piperine)

foods_to_avoid.food: High-FODMAP Foods — FRUCTANS (Wheat, Rye, Garlic, Onion, Leek)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Fructans are chains of fructose molecules that cannot be digested by human intestinal enzymes — they reach the colon intact and are rapidly fermented by bacteria producing large quantities of hydrogen and methane gas, causing bloating, pain, flatulence, and altered stool consistency. GARLIC and ONION are the MOST potent FODMAP triggers in most IBS patients — even small amounts in cooking (garlic-infused oil is LOW FODMAP as fructans are not oil-soluble).
examples: Garlic (any amount — extremely high fructan content; use garlic-infused oil instead)
Onion (white, red, brown, spring onion bulb — extremely high fructan)
Wheat-based products: regular bread, pasta, pizza dough, pastries, cakes, biscuits
Products containing inulin or FOS (chicory root extract — added prebiotic fibre; very high FODMAP)

foods_to_avoid.reason: These fruits contain excess fructose (more fructose than glucose — excess fructose is poorly absorbed in the small intestine in many individuals; ratio of fructose to glucose >1:1 impairs absorption via GLUT5 transporter which has limited capacity)
examples: Dried fruits (raisins, sultanas, dates, figs — very concentrated FODMAP)
Tinned fruit in apple or pear juice

foods_to_avoid.reason: Lactose (milk disaccharide) requires lactase enzyme for digestion — deficiency (common in South Asians, East Asians, Africans, Middle Eastern populations — up to 80% adult prevalence of lactase persistence loss) causes osmotic and fermentative diarrhoea with gas and bloating
examples: Yogurt (regular — especially natural/plain yogurt; Greek yogurt is lower lactose)
Soft cheeses: ricotta, cottage cheese, fresh mozzarella, cream cheese
foods_to_avoid.alternatives: Lactose-free milk, lactose-free yogurt, hard aged cheeses (cheddar, parmesan, brie — naturally low lactose), plant-based milks (check for added high-FODMAP ingredients)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Dietary fat delays gastric emptying and stimulates the gastrocolic reflex — the post-prandial increase in colonic motility that triggers urgency and diarrhoea in IBS-D. Fat also promotes gastric acid production and CCK release which can worsen IBS symptoms. High-fat meals are a primary trigger for post-prandial cramping.

Caffeine stimulates colonic motility (increases HAPCs — high-amplitude propagated contractions); exacerbates urgency and diarrhoea in IBS-D; may worsen abdominal cramping; promotes anxiety (worsening gut-brain axis dysfunction)
examples: Coffee (regular — significant caffeine; decaffeinated coffee also stimulates gut transit to lesser degree from non-caffeine components)
foods_to_avoid.note: Green tea (moderate caffeine) is generally better tolerated than coffee in IBS

foods_to_avoid.reason: Alcohol disrupts gut microbiome (dysbiosis); increases intestinal permeability (leaky gut — important in IBS pathogenesis); accelerates gut transit causing diarrhoea; is directly irritating to gut mucosa; promotes anxiety (worsening gut-brain axis)
examples: Beer (high in FODMAPs — fructans from barley + alcohol)
Spirits (alcohol alone — lower FODMAP but still gut-disruptive)
foods_to_avoid.note: Beer is particularly problematic — fructans from barley malting + alcohol combined

foods_to_avoid.reason: Artificial sweeteners — particularly polyols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol, erythritol, maltitol, isomalt) — are poorly absorbed in the small intestine and cause osmotic diarrhoea and bloating. Labelled as 'sugar-free', 'diet', 'diabetic', or 'low-calorie' on products.
examples: Sugar-free chewing gum and mints (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol)
Some protein bars and supplements (maltitol, sorbitol)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Legumes contain galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS — alpha-galactosides like raffinose and stachyose) which are completely non-digestible and highly fermentable, producing enormous quantities of gas
examples: Regular beans: kidney beans, black beans, chickpeas (DRIED and COOKED)
foods_to_avoid.lower_FODMAP_options: Tinned chickpeas and lentils (drained and rinsed — ¼ cup); tofu (firm); tempeh

foods_to_avoid.reason: Capsaicin activates TRPV1 pain receptors in the intestinal mucosa — directly lowers visceral pain threshold and worsens abdominal cramping; also accelerates transit time in IBS-D; reduces anal sphincter relaxation pressure (may worsen urgency)
examples: Strong black pepper in large amounts

sample_meal_plan.note: This low-FODMAP IBS-friendly meal plan avoids common triggers while providing complete nutrition. Individual tolerance varies — use this as a starting point and adjust based on personal food diary. Consult a registered dietitian specialising in IBS for personalised guidance before starting the full low-FODMAP diet.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: 1 cup warm ginger tea (fresh ginger — 1-2cm in hot water) — antispasmodic; anti-nausea; settles gut before breakfast
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal (plain rolled oats) with strawberries (10), blueberries (handful), and 2 tablespoons maple syrup or 1 tablespoon peanut butter (no xylitol) + lactose-free milk OR scrambled eggs (2) on gluten-free toast (1-2 slices) + 1 kiwi
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: 1 medium orange or 15 grapes + small handful rice crackers with peanut butter (check no high-FODMAP additives) + 1 cup herbal tea (chamomile or peppermint — if no GERD)
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Rice (brown or white) + plain grilled chicken or firm tofu + low-FODMAP vegetable curry/stir-fry (courgette, carrot, bell pepper, spinach, tomato) cooked with garlic-infused oil (NOT garlic) and spices (cumin, coriander, turmeric — low FODMAP) + lactose-free plain yogurt (50-100g)
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: Plain rice cakes (2-3) with a small amount of cheddar cheese or peanut butter + 1 cup ginger or peppermint herbal tea
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Grilled fish or chicken + 1 medium portion of cooked quinoa or rice + green beans, carrots, and courgette (steamed or baked) + olive oil and lemon dressing (no garlic, no onion, no HFCS)
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: Small cup warm chamomile tea or peppermint tea; avoid eating for 2-3 hours before bed

special_dietary_notes: LOW FODMAP DIET MUST BE DONE WITH A DIETITIAN — self-implementing without professional guidance risks nutritional deficiencies, unnecessary restriction, and misidentification of triggers. The diet is complex and requires careful guidance through all 3 phases.
