SOLUBLE FIBRE (psyllium husk/ispaghula) is the most evidence-based fibre supplement for IBS — improves both constipation AND diarrhoea (BRAN/INSOLUBLE FIBRE often WORSENS IBS symptoms — common clinical mistake)

GARLIC-INFUSED OIL is a low-FODMAP alternative to garlic — FODMAP fructans are not fat-soluble and do not leach into oil; frying garlic cloves in oil and removing them leaves a flavoured, low-FODMAP oil suitable for IBS

COOKING ONION with other vegetables does NOT reduce FODMAP content — FODMAPs are water-soluble and leach into any dish cooked with onions; use spring onion (scallion) GREEN TOPS only (low FODMAP) instead
REGULAR MEAL TIMES are protective for IBS — irregular meals worsen gut motility patterns; aim for 3 regular meals and 1-2 snacks at consistent times
EATING SLOWLY and not over-eating protects against triggering the gastrocolic reflex — large meals trigger more post-prandial cramping
FOOD DIARY for 2-4 weeks before dietitian appointment: record food and drink, portion sizes, and timing of symptoms — identifies personal triggers efficiently

Prebiotic FODMAPs (garlic, onion, wheat) actually feed beneficial gut bacteria — prolonged strict avoidance may reduce microbiome diversity. Phase 3 personalisation aims to reintroduce tolerated FODMAPs to restore prebiotic function

psychological_therapies.overview: Psychological therapies are among the MOST EFFECTIVE treatments for IBS — comparable or superior to pharmacotherapy, particularly for moderate-severe IBS. The ACG 2021 guidelines give a STRONG recommendation for psychological therapies for global IBS symptoms. The gut-brain axis is central to IBS pathophysiology — psychological therapies directly modify this axis.

therapies.description: Structured psychological therapy addressing: catastrophising (exaggerated fear of symptoms), hypervigilance to gut sensations, avoidance behaviours (avoiding food, social activities, travel due to IBS fear), and maladaptive coping. Both face-to-face (most effective) and online/self-directed formats have evidence.
therapies.evidence: Multiple RCTs demonstrate CBT reduces IBS symptom severity by 40-50% vs control; sustained benefits at 12 months; equally effective for all IBS subtypes
therapies.format: 6-12 sessions (individual or group); also accessible via online platforms (e.g., Nerva, Cara Care)

therapies.description: Specialised hypnotherapy focusing specifically on the gut — induces deep relaxation and uses gut-specific visualisation and suggestions to calm the gut-brain connection, reduce visceral hypersensitivity, and alter gut motility. The 'Manchester Protocol' by Peter Whorwell is the most studied format.
therapies.evidence: Whorwell et al. landmark studies: GDH achieved complete or near-complete remission in 80-90% of IBS patients; superior to medical therapy alone; sustained at 5-year follow-up; particularly effective for refractory IBS; NNT approximately 3-4
therapies.format: 7-12 weekly sessions (individual hypnotherapist or self-directed audio); Nerva app (evidence-based gut hypnotherapy app)

therapies.therapy: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) / Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT)
therapies.description: Teaches present-moment non-judgemental awareness of physical sensations including gut symptoms — reduces 'catastrophising' and hypervigilance; reduces HPA axis stress activation; improves pain tolerance and acceptance
therapies.evidence: Multiple RCTs show significant IBS symptom improvement; particularly beneficial for IBS with comorbid anxiety and stress-related worsening

therapies.description: Addresses underlying psychological conflicts, interpersonal difficulties, and unresolved trauma contributing to IBS — particularly relevant when history of abuse or significant life stressors are present
therapies.evidence: Effective for severe refractory IBS and IBS with psychological comorbidities

therapies.description: For IBS-C with pelvic floor dyssynergia — uses biofeedback equipment to teach patients to relax the pelvic floor muscles during defecation (paradoxical contraction is the abnormality). Also addresses defaecation posture (squatting vs seated position affects ano-rectal angle).
therapies.evidence: 75-80% improvement in straining and incomplete evacuation in pelvic floor dyssynergia when biofeedback is correctly targeted

exercise.evidence: Multiple RCTs demonstrate regular physical activity improves global IBS symptoms, reduces psychological distress, and reduces GI transit time (beneficial in IBS-C). Exercise reduces visceral hypersensitivity via central mechanisms and improves gut microbiome diversity.
recommendations: 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week (walking, cycling, swimming)
Regular exercise reduces IBS symptoms by 43% in trials; improves quality of life, fatigue, and psychological wellbeing
Yoga — evidence for IBS symptom improvement through combined exercise, breathing, and stress reduction; particularly useful for IBS with anxiety
Walking after meals reduces post-prandial bloating and assists gastric emptying
Avoid intense exercise immediately after eating (increases post-prandial GI symptoms)

sleep_hygiene.importance: Sleep disturbance and IBS are bidirectionally related. Poor sleep amplifies gut pain sensitivity via increased visceral hypersensitivity the following day; gut symptoms at night (discomfort, anxiety about next-day symptoms) impair sleep quality. Improving sleep reduces IBS severity.
measures: Consistent sleep and wake times — 7-8 hours per night
Avoid large meals within 3 hours of bedtime
Establish a pre-sleep relaxation routine (avoid screens; reading; warm bath)
CBT for Insomnia (CBT-I) if insomnia is prominent — evidence-based treatment for sleep disorders in chronic pain conditions
Amitriptyline at night (when prescribed) — sedation can be harnessed to improve sleep AND treat IBS simultaneously

stress_management_techniques: Daily diaphragmatic (belly) breathing — 5-10 minutes: activates parasympathetic nervous system; directly reduces gut-brain axis stress reactivity; reduces HPA axis activation
Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) — 15 minutes daily; reduces overall sympathetic nervous system tone
Regular social activity — social isolation worsens IBS through increased rumination and symptom focus; maintaining social connections is protective
Journalling — writing about symptoms and emotional experiences reduces symptom severity (expressive writing studies); reduces catastrophising
Time management and reducing work overload — occupational stress is a major IBS trigger; boundary-setting and workload management
bowel_habit_retraining: Establish a regular toilet time — use the natural post-breakfast gastrocolic reflex (the increase in colonic motility after waking and eating breakfast) to train a consistent morning defecation time
NEVER suppress the urge to defecate (IBS-D) — holding urges trains the bowel to be less responsive
NEVER strain at stool (IBS-C) — use a squat stool (Squatty Potty) to optimise the anorectal angle; lean forward with feet on stool
Defecation posture: knees higher than hips (squatting position) relaxes the puborectalis muscle and straightens the anorectal angle — improves evacuation efficiency
Allow adequate time in the bathroom without rushing or phone distraction
ibs_education_and_acceptance: Understanding IBS as a real, physiological disorder (not 'all in your head') significantly reduces health anxiety and improves outcomes — education IS treatment
Reassurance that IBS does NOT cause bowel cancer, does NOT progress to IBD (Crohn's/UC), and does NOT shorten life expectancy
Acknowledging that IBS is chronic and relapsing-remitting — good periods and flares are expected; catastrophising during flares worsens them
IBS support organisations: IBS Network (UK — theibsnetwork.org); IFFGD (USA); The Gut Health Doctor; online IBS communities provide peer support and validated information
Symptom tracking app — use a validated IBS tracking app (mySymptoms, Cara) to track symptoms, food, stress, sleep, and menstrual cycle — identifies patterns and triggers

ibs_monitoring_plan.note: IBS monitoring tracks symptom severity, treatment response, alarm feature development, and quality of life impact. The IBS Symptom Severity Score (IBS-SSS) is the validated tool for objective monitoring — complete at baseline and 4-8 weekly intervals. Keep a symptom and food diary throughout treatment.

green_zone.status: Well Managed — Mild Symptoms or Remission
green_zone.criteria: IBS-SSS <175; symptoms on <25% of days; manageable with dietary modifications and PRN antispasmodics; no significant impact on work, social life, or sleep; patient feels in control of their IBS; no alarm features
green_zone.action: Continue low FODMAP diet (in Phase 3 personalisation); continue exercise and stress management; use PRN antispasmodics (mebeverine, peppermint oil) for flares; annual GP review; reassess medications annually with aim to reduce where possible. Maintain a headache diary to track triggers.

yellow_zone.criteria: IBS-SSS 175-300; symptoms affecting work or social activities; requiring regular (not just PRN) medication; anxiety about IBS increasing; low FODMAP diet inadequate alone; new or changing symptom pattern
yellow_zone.action: GP or gastroenterology review within 2-4 weeks. Reassess IBS subtype and current treatment. Consider: adding regular antispasmodic; IBS-D: trial loperamide or rifaximin; IBS-C: linaclotide or prucalopride; all: low-dose amitriptyline or SSRI; psychological therapy referral (CBT or gut-directed hypnotherapy). Review food diary with dietitian.

red_zone.status: URGENT — Alarm Features or Severe Refractory IBS
red_zone.criteria_urgent: ANY of: Rectal bleeding (bright red or blood mixed with stool); Unintentional weight loss >5%; Iron-deficiency anaemia (new); Nocturnal diarrhoea consistently waking patient; Fever with GI symptoms; New symptom onset after age 50; Progressive worsening not explained by IBS; Palpable abdominal mass
red_zone.criteria_specialist: IBS-SSS >300 with failed multiple treatments; severe urgency with faecal incontinence; severe refractory constipation not responding to secretagogues; significant psychological comorbidity requiring multidisciplinary care
red_zone.action: ALARM FEATURES: Urgent GP review within days; urgent referral for colonoscopy/endoscopy; 2-week wait cancer referral if suspicion of malignancy. SEVERE REFRACTORY IBS: Gastroenterology specialist referral; psychological therapy referral; faecal calprotectin; consideration of colonoscopy with biopsies; SeHCAT test (IBS-D); anorectal physiology if IBS-C with outlet dysfunction.

complications.complication: Severe Impairment of Quality of Life
complications.description: IBS does not cause structural bowel damage but profoundly and chronically impairs quality of life — to an extent comparable or exceeding many 'serious' organic diseases. Studies show HRQL (health-related quality of life) in severe IBS is comparable to patients on dialysis for renal failure, patients with multiple sclerosis, and patients awaiting organ transplantation. Multiple life domains affected: work productivity, social activities, travel, eating out, relationships, sexual health, and mental health.
domains_affected: Work absence (absenteeism) and presenteeism (at work but reduced productivity)
Social avoidance — cancelling plans, avoiding restaurants, events, travel
Dietary restriction — social stigma of food avoidance
Sexual dysfunction from pelvic pain and dyspareunia
Relationship strain from chronic illness impact
Travel anxiety and restriction (fear of being away from toilets)

complications.complication: Mental Health Comorbidities — Anxiety and Depression
complications.description: Anxiety and depression are both MORE COMMON in IBS and WORSEN IBS — a bidirectional relationship. Prevalence: moderate-severe anxiety in 60% of IBS clinic patients; depression in 40%. The gut-brain axis dysregulation underlying IBS shares mechanisms with anxiety and depression disorders (HPA axis, serotonin signalling, central sensitisation). Mental health disorders amplify visceral pain and worsen functional outcomes.
complications.severity: Significant — must be treated concurrently with GI symptoms
complications.management: Screen all IBS patients for depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7); refer to psychological therapies; CBT; low-dose antidepressants (dual benefit for GI and psychiatric symptoms)

complications.description: A concerning complication of IBS — particularly in women with chronic pelvic pain and IBS — is unnecessarily high rates of abdominal surgery. Studies show IBS patients have 2-3x higher rates of cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal), appendectomy, hysterectomy, and other abdominal procedures compared to non-IBS populations — many of which are performed to treat symptoms later identified as IBS-related. This represents significant unnecessary surgical risk.
complications.prevention: Positive IBS diagnosis BEFORE referring for surgery; second opinion from gastroenterologist before any elective abdominal surgery in patient with IBS-like symptoms; pelvic pain in women with IBS requires careful evaluation before gynaecological surgery

complications.description: Overly restrictive diets in IBS — particularly self-implemented low FODMAP diets without dietitian guidance, or very restricted 'safe food' lists — can lead to: calcium deficiency (dairy avoidance), iron deficiency (meat and legume avoidance), B12 deficiency (animal product restriction), vitamin D deficiency, fibre deficiency (low FODMAP may reduce prebiotic fibre), and reduced gut microbiome diversity.
complications.prevention: Dietitian-guided dietary management; Phase 3 FODMAP personalisation (maximise diet liberalisation); regular nutritional review; supplementation as needed

complications.description: Long-term use of opioid antidiarrhoeal agents (loperamide at high doses) can cause dependency and constipation. Laxative dependency in IBS-C is possible with stimulant laxatives. Benzodiazepine use for IBS-related anxiety creates addiction risk. Opioid analgesics prescribed for chronic IBS pain cause narcotic bowel syndrome (opioid-induced gut hypersensitivity — paradoxical worsening of pain with opioid use).
complications.prevention: Avoid opioid analgesics for IBS; use non-addictive antidiarrhoeals (loperamide at recommended doses); review all long-term medications annually

complications.description: IBS frequently overlaps with other functional and chronic pain conditions — all sharing central sensitisation mechanisms: Fibromyalgia (30-40% of IBS patients), Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/ME (20-30%), Interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome (30%), Chronic pelvic pain (30% women), Chronic low back pain, Temporomandibular disorder (TMD), Migraine. This overlap creates a complex clinical picture requiring multidisciplinary management.
complications.management: Multidisciplinary team approach; central sensitisation-targeting treatments (low-dose TCAs, SNRIs, CBT, MBCT, aerobic exercise) benefit multiple overlapping conditions simultaneously

complications.description: Severe IBS patients may progressively restrict social activities, avoid eating out with friends or family, decline travel, and withdraw from relationships — due to fear of symptom flares, urgency, flatulence, or needing rapid toilet access. Social isolation worsens depression and anxiety, creating a vicious cycle. Partners may face secondary burden from caring for chronically unwell individual with invisible illness.
complications.management: CBT addresses avoidance behaviours specifically; IBS-specific support groups; communication strategies for explaining IBS to partners and employers; graduated exposure to feared situations (restaurants, travel, social events)

key_points: IBS affects women 2-3 times more than men in high-income countries; the sex difference is driven by hormonal factors, differences in gut motility, heightened pain perception, and higher rates of healthcare-seeking behaviour

Menstrual cycle: IBS symptoms fluctuate across the menstrual cycle — premenstrual and menstrual phases cause greatest symptom worsening (prostaglandins — IBS-D worsening; progesterone — IBS-C worsening in luteal phase); track symptoms alongside menstrual cycle in IBS diary

Dysmenorrhoea and pelvic pain frequently overlap with IBS — endometriosis must be excluded in women with severe IBS-like symptoms and pelvic pain before treating as IBS (endometriosis affects 10% of women; common coexistence with IBS)

Pregnancy: IBS often improves in pregnancy (reduced stress hormones; altered gut microbiome); postpartum relapse common; treat with safe options during pregnancy (fibre, peppermint oil, limited loperamide in 2nd/3rd trimester); avoid serotonin-modulating drugs in 1st trimester
Menopause: IBS may worsen in perimenopause (oestrogen reduction affects gut motility and visceral pain threshold); HRT may modestly improve GI symptoms in some postmenopausal women
Female-specific pharmacotherapy: lubiprostone (IBS-C — approved only for women); alosetron (IBS-D — approved only for women in USA)
Paediatric IBS is increasingly prevalent — affects 10-20% of school-age children and adolescents
School avoidance from IBS is an important red flag — must distinguish IBS-driven school avoidance from anxiety-driven school refusal (though both often coexist)

Rome IV Paediatric Criteria: abdominal pain ≥4 days/month, ≥2 months duration, with ≥2 of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form; 'associated symptoms' include bloating and visible abdominal distension
Family-based approach is essential — parents' anxiety about symptoms amplifies children's symptoms; family therapy and psychoeducation alongside patient education

Dietary management: low FODMAP diet with dietitian in older children (12+); younger children benefit from simpler dietary advice (regular meals, adequate water, avoid skipping meals, limit fizzy drinks)

Medication: avoid low-dose TCAs in children under 12 (limited evidence, anticholinergic concerns); peppermint oil capsules safe from age 8; psyllium fibre safe; probiotics (Lactobacillus GG) evidence-based in paediatric IBS
Psychological therapies highly effective in children — CBT, mindfulness, gut-directed hypnotherapy; parental involvement in therapy

New onset of IBS-like symptoms after age 50 should ALWAYS be investigated to exclude organic disease (colorectal cancer, IBD, microscopic colitis, coeliac disease, diverticular disease) — lower threshold for colonoscopy
Medication interactions more significant in elderly polypharmacy — many IBS drugs interact with common elderly medications
Anticholinergic burden: avoid hyoscine, dicyclomine, and high-dose TCAs in elderly (high anticholinergic burden worsens cognition; higher fall risk from orthostatic hypotension)
Prefer: mebeverine (no anticholinergic), peppermint oil, low-dose nortriptyline (fewer anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline), prucalopride (IBS-C)
Faecal calprotectin is particularly important in elderly new-onset GI symptoms — escalated investigation threshold

Microscopic colitis (collagenous or lymphocytic colitis) is a common cause of IBS-D in older women — requires colonoscopy with biopsies for diagnosis (endoscopy appears normal; diagnosis only on biopsy); treat with budesonide
PI-IBS is a distinct entity with specific aetiology — Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, norovirus, rotavirus, Giardia are the most common precipitating pathogens
Risk factors for PI-IBS after gastroenteritis: female sex, younger age, severe initial infection, anxiety/depression at time of infection, antibiotic treatment
Approximately 10-15% of patients who experience acute gastroenteritis develop PI-IBS
Prognosis: PI-IBS tends to improve over time (spontaneous resolution in ~50% at 6 years) — importantly different from non-PI-IBS which is typically a lifelong relapsing-remitting condition
Probiotics particularly rationale in PI-IBS — microbiome disruption is a proven mechanism; Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or multi-strain probiotics
Rifaximin may be particularly effective in PI-IBS (targets SIBO which can be precipitated by gastroenteritis)
Exclude ongoing infective cause (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) before diagnosing PI-IBS — stool OCP testing essential

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Viral illnesses including influenza significantly worsen IBS through multiple mechanisms: systemic immune activation increases gut mucosal immune activity and visceral hypersensitivity; fever affects gut motility; physical stress triggers IBS flares. Influenza has been documented as a trigger for post-infectious IBS. Annual vaccination reduces both flu illness and IBS exacerbations triggered by flu. Patients with severe IBS and comorbid anxiety are particularly vulnerable to illness-triggered flares.

COVID-19 infection causes significant gut symptoms — the GI tract expresses ACE2 receptors that SARS-CoV-2 binds directly. Post-COVID GI sequelae include new or worsened IBS-like symptoms (post-COVID IBS has been documented as a post-infectious IBS variant). COVID illness triggers major IBS flares through systemic inflammation and psychological stress. Vaccination protects against severe COVID-19 and reduces post-COVID gut dysfunction risk.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose course (0, 6-12 months); for travellers and at-risk individuals
vaccinations_recommended.reason: IBS patients frequently travel anxiously — they are more likely to visit remote destinations to 'test' their IBS. Hepatitis A (transmitted through contaminated food and water) causes severe acute hepatitis but can also trigger post-infectious IBS after the acute illness resolves. Travellers with IBS should be up to date with Hepatitis A vaccination before international travel.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Twinrix (combined Hep A + B) recommended for travellers requiring both

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Every 3 years (oral Ty21a) or single injection (Vi polysaccharide) for travel to endemic areas
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Salmonella Typhi (typhoid) is a well-documented precipitant of post-infectious IBS (PI-IBS). IBS patients who develop typhoid after travel are at higher risk of PI-IBS development than those without pre-existing IBS predisposition. Typhoid vaccination before travel to South Asia, Africa, and Southeast Asia prevents typhoid and its potential gut-brain axis sequelae.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Oral vaccine — 2-3 doses from 6 weeks of age per childhood immunisation schedule
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Rotavirus is a common precipitant of paediatric post-infectious IBS. Children who suffer severe rotavirus gastroenteritis have increased rates of IBS development in childhood and adolescence. Rotavirus vaccination dramatically reduces severe gastroenteritis in children and thus reduces the burden of post-infectious IBS in childhood.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-3 doses per national schedule for adolescents; catch-up to age 26
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Chronic pelvic pain from HPV-related cervical lesions or treatment (LLETZ) shares mechanisms with IBS-related pelvic pain and can worsen IBS. While not directly treating IBS, HPV vaccination prevents future gynaecological pathology that may overlap with and worsen pelvic IBS symptoms in women.

Mpox causes GI symptoms and proctitis (rectal IBS-like pain and altered bowel habits) — relevant to IBS patients with rectal involvement who may misattribute mpox proctitis to their IBS. Vaccination in eligible high-risk groups prevents mpox and its GI complications that could trigger or mimic IBS exacerbations.

when_to_see_doctor: First presentation with recurrent abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits lasting more than 4-6 weeks — formal IBS diagnosis, exclusion of organic disease, and management planning required
Rectal bleeding or blood mixed in stool — ALARM FEATURE — must not be attributed to IBS without investigation (haemorrhoids are common but rectal bleeding always requires examination)
Unintentional weight loss (more than 2-3 kg without intentional dieting) — alarm feature requiring urgent investigation
Symptoms starting after age 50 years — higher index of suspicion for organic disease; colonoscopy should be considered
Nocturnal symptoms consistently waking you from sleep (diarrhoea or severe pain) — unlike typical IBS; requires investigation for IBD or other organic cause
Symptoms not responding after 4-8 weeks of dietary changes and first-line treatments (antispasmodics, loperamide, fibre)
IBS significantly impacting work attendance, social life, or mental health (IBS-SSS >175) — specialist gastroenterology or IBS nurse referral warranted
New or changing symptoms in a previously stable IBS patient — change from pattern warrants reassessment
Concern about iron deficiency (extreme tiredness, pallor, breathlessness) in a patient with IBS-D — iron deficiency anaemia is an alarm feature
Severe anxiety or depression accompanying IBS — psychological therapy and possible antidepressant treatment
Women with IBS and severe pelvic pain — endometriosis should be excluded before attributing all symptoms to IBS
Faecal incontinence — despite IBS urgency, frank incontinence requires specialist anorectal assessment
Before starting any new IBS medication — to discuss options, tailoring to subtype, and monitoring plan
emergency_signs: Sudden severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, or shock — possible bowel perforation, ischaemia, or another surgical emergency — IBS DOES NOT CAUSE THESE — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY
Frank rectal bleeding — large amounts of bright red blood per rectum — possible lower GI haemorrhage from colorectal cancer, diverticular bleed, or vascular malformation — EMERGENCY
Black tarry stools (melaena) — upper GI bleeding — EMERGENCY
Severe abdominal pain with fever and rigidity — possible peritonitis or bowel obstruction — EMERGENCY

Sudden severe worsening of IBS symptoms with fever, blood PR, and rapid deterioration over hours to days — possible new inflammatory bowel disease, infective colitis, or ischaemic colitis presenting acutely — URGENT EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT
Severe dehydration from prolonged diarrhoea (dry mouth, no urination, collapse) — seek emergency care
Confusion or altered consciousness with GI symptoms — possible metabolic disturbance (severe electrolyte loss) or alternative serious diagnosis

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is IBS and why do I get it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: IBS (Irritable Bowel Syndrome) is a chronic condition affecting how the gut works — specifically the gut-brain connection. In IBS, the communication system between your brain and gut is dysregulated, making the gut overly sensitive and reactive. This causes the gut to respond excessively to normal stimuli like food, stress, or mild bloating that most people wouldn't notice. IBS is real, physiological, and not 'all in your head' — but it is genuinely influenced by both gut function and the nervous system. Causes include: genetics, gut-brain axis dysfunction, altered gut microbiome, previous gut infections, food sensitivities (particularly to FODMAPs), and psychological stress — which is why it's considered a biopsychosocial condition.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Does IBS cause cancer or progress to a more serious disease like Crohn's?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No — IBS does NOT cause bowel cancer, does NOT progress to Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis (IBD), and does NOT cause permanent structural damage to the intestine. The gut lining in IBS is functionally abnormal but structurally normal (though there may be subtle microscopic immune changes). IBS does NOT shorten life expectancy. While IBS is chronic and can be very debilitating to quality of life, it is NOT dangerous in the way that cancers or inflammatory bowel diseases are. This is an important reassurance that significantly reduces anxiety-driven symptom amplification when patients understand it.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the Low FODMAP Diet and should I try it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The Low FODMAP Diet eliminates FODMAPs — Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides And Polyols — short-chain carbohydrates that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine and cause bloating, gas, pain, and altered bowel habits in IBS. Common high-FODMAP foods include: garlic, onion, wheat bread, apples, pears, milk, and many legumes. The diet has three phases: elimination (4-8 weeks), reintroduction (6-8 weeks — testing each FODMAP group individually), and personalisation (long-term tailored diet). Evidence shows 50-75% of IBS patients improve significantly on it. IMPORTANT: always do this diet with a dietitian — doing it alone risks nutritional deficiency and excessive restriction.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is my IBS related to stress? Can stress cause IBS?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Absolutely — stress and IBS are deeply connected through the gut-brain axis. Psychological stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and releases stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) that directly affect gut motility, gut sensitivity, and intestinal permeability. Stress is the most consistently reported IBS trigger. However, IBS is NOT 'just stress' — there are genuine physiological changes in the gut (altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity, microbiome changes) that are not simply 'in your mind'. The relationship is bidirectional: IBS symptoms cause anxiety and stress, which then worsen the symptoms. This is why psychological therapies (CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy) are among the MOST effective IBS treatments.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the most effective treatment for IBS?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No single treatment works for everyone — IBS management is highly individual. The most effective overall approaches: (1) Low FODMAP diet with a specialist dietitian — 50-75% of patients improve significantly; (2) Psychological therapies — CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy achieve comparable or better results than medications for moderate-severe IBS; (3) Gut-directed hypnotherapy — 80-90% improvement in clinical studies; (4) Low-dose amitriptyline (10-75mg at night) — strongest pharmacological evidence for reducing IBS pain; (5) Peppermint oil (enteric-coated capsules) — evidence-based antispasmodic. In practice, combining dietary intervention, lifestyle changes (exercise, stress management), and targeted medication gives the best outcomes. NICE recommends trying dietary measures first, then pharmacotherapy, then psychological therapies if not improving — though often all three are used simultaneously.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between IBS and IBD (Crohn's or Ulcerative Colitis)?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: IBS and IBD are completely different conditions despite similar-sounding abbreviations. IBS (Irritable Bowel Syndrome): a functional disorder — the bowel looks normal on endoscopy, no ulcers, no erosions; no bleeding; no significant inflammation; not associated with cancer; does not shorten life; managed mainly with diet, lifestyle, and medications. IBD (Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Crohn's disease or Ulcerative Colitis): a structural disease — visible inflammation, ulcers, and erosions on endoscopy; can cause rectal bleeding; associated with increased cancer risk in long-term disease; requires immunosuppressive medications; can shorten life if severely uncontrolled. Key distinguishing features: blood in stool (IBD, not IBS), elevated faecal calprotectin (IBD, not IBS), weight loss and anaemia (IBD), nocturnal diarrhoea (IBD more than IBS), and normal endoscopy (IBS).

frequently_asked_questions.question: I have IBS-D with constant diarrhoea and urgency — what treatments specifically help?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: For IBS-D (diarrhoea-predominant), the following evidence-based treatments are most helpful: (1) Low FODMAP diet — particularly restricting lactose (dairy) and fructans (wheat, garlic, onion); (2) Loperamide (Imodium) 2-4mg before anticipated trigger situations (meals, going out) — reduces urgency and stool frequency; (3) Peppermint oil enteric-coated capsules — antispasmodic for cramping and urgency; (4) Low-dose amitriptyline (10-25mg at night) — slows gut transit AND reduces visceral pain; (5) Rifaximin (550mg TDS for 14 days) if bloating is prominent; (6) Ondansetron (4-8mg daily off-label) — reduces urgency and improves stool consistency; (7) Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine) if bile acid malabsorption (BAM) diagnosed. Also crucially: ensure coeliac disease has been excluded (blood test) and Giardia (stool antigen test).

frequently_asked_questions.question: I have IBS-C — what can I take for the constipation and pain?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: For IBS-C (constipation-predominant), the key is treating BOTH constipation AND pain simultaneously — regular constipation treatments like Lactulose only address stool consistency, not pain. Evidence-based IBS-C treatments: (1) Linaclotide (Constella/Linzess) — prescription secretagogue; reduces BOTH constipation AND abdominal pain (the only treatment type to do both); take 30-60 minutes before breakfast; (2) Psyllium husk (ispaghula/Isabgol) — soluble fibre; take with lots of water; improves stool consistency and reduces pain; (3) Prucalopride — accelerates colonic transit; once daily; (4) Polyethylene glycol (Movicol) — osmotic laxative for constipation; less bloating than lactulose; (5) Peppermint oil capsules — antispasmodic for cramping; (6) Low FODMAP diet tailored for IBS-C (avoid fructans, lactose); (7) Low-dose fluoxetine or citalopram (SSRIs accelerate gut transit — beneficial in IBS-C). Adequate water intake (2 litres daily) is essential with any constipation treatment.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can probiotics help IBS?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — probiotics have moderate evidence for IBS symptom improvement in clinical trials. A Cochrane meta-analysis found probiotics significantly better than placebo for global IBS symptoms and bloating. The key caveat: effects are strain-specific. Not all probiotics are the same. Best-evidenced strains for IBS: (1) Bifidobacterium longum 35624 (Align/Alflorex) — strongest evidence for IBS pain, bloating, and bowel habits; (2) VSL#3 (14-strain high-potency) — evidence for bloating specifically; (3) Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG — evidence in PI-IBS and paediatric IBS; (4) Saccharomyces boulardii — IBS-D. Trial a probiotic for 4-8 weeks — if beneficial, continue; if no benefit, try a different strain. Some patients notice initial increased gas in first 1-2 weeks as microbiome adjusts — this typically settles.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My doctor wants to prescribe amitriptyline for IBS — I'm not depressed. Why?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: This is an extremely common and important question. Amitriptyline is being prescribed for IBS at a MUCH LOWER DOSE than it is used for depression (10-75mg vs 150-300mg for depression). At this low dose, amitriptyline works as a PAIN MODULATOR and gut motility modifier — not as an antidepressant. It works by: reducing abnormal gut pain signalling (central sensitisation), slowing intestinal transit (beneficial for IBS-D), improving sleep quality, and reducing visceral hypersensitivity. Multiple clinical trials prove its effectiveness for IBS abdominal pain — it is one of the most evidence-based pharmacological treatments for IBS pain. Studies show 70-80% of IBS patients prescribed low-dose amitriptyline benefit. Please do not refuse this medication based on the assumption it means you are being diagnosed with depression — it's a fundamentally different use.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods should I definitely avoid with IBS?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The most common IBS food triggers are: (1) GARLIC and ONION — the most potent triggers for most IBS patients (high fructans); use garlic-infused oil instead; (2) Wheat-based products (bread, pasta, pizza) — fructans in wheat; try gluten-free alternatives; (3) Dairy products containing lactose (milk, soft cheese, ice cream) — use lactose-free or hard cheeses; (4) Apples, pears, mango — high fructose; replace with berries, oranges, kiwi; (5) Legumes in large amounts (chickpeas, lentils, beans) — high GOS; use rinsed tinned versions in small portions; (6) Caffeine — coffee, strong tea; (7) Alcohol (especially beer); (8) Carbonated fizzy drinks; (9) Spicy foods; (10) Large meals. Individual triggers VARY ENORMOUSLY — keep a food diary and ideally work with a dietitian to do the full Low FODMAP elimination and reintroduction programme to identify YOUR specific triggers.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is gut-directed hypnotherapy and does it work for IBS?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Gut-directed hypnotherapy (GDH) is a specialised form of clinical hypnotherapy where a trained therapist (or structured audio programme) induces a deep relaxation state and uses gut-specific visualisations, suggestions, and imagery to calm the gut-brain connection, reduce visceral hypersensitivity, alter gut motility, and improve psychological wellbeing. It is NOT stage hypnosis — you are fully in control throughout. The Manchester Protocol by Peter Whorwell and colleagues at Salford Royal is the most extensively studied format. Evidence: GDH achieves complete or near-complete IBS symptom remission in 80-90% of patients in clinical trials — one of the highest success rates of any IBS treatment. Benefits are sustained at 5-year follow-up in 73% of patients. It is now recommended in UK NICE and AGA guidelines. The Nerva app provides evidence-based self-directed gut hypnotherapy and is a practical accessible option.
